reply.summary: Wrote docs/designs/026-registry-service/01-research.md for ADR-026, grounded in the source ADR plus its cited ledger (013, 021, 022, 023, 025), the shipped client and match store (apps/discovery-cli/src/catalog.rs, matches.rs), the gate suite, the formats contract (schemas/README.md) and the harness tests that sweep schemas/*/v*/. Three lenses applied — prior art (Docker Distribution pull-through cache, Verdaccio uplinks, nginx proxy_cache_use_stale, IGDB external_games, Wikidata P1733, MusicBrainz), security landscape (RFC 6750's mandatory-TLS posture versus 026-R1's plaintext bearer admin face, the plaintext upstream hop as an identity-injection path into cache-v1.json and the match store, RFC 9112 framing and slow-low exposure, the loopback auto-enable rule), and standards (RFC 9110 status/method semantics for the 404/405/503 choices, RFC 5861 stale serving, RFC 3986 encoding, RFC 6335 ephemeral ports). Two concrete blockers surfaced for the designer: 026-B1 (5,000 cache entries) against 026-B2 (1 MiB) does not close given the uncapped per-entry candidate payload under MAX_CANDIDATES, and a schemas/catalog/v1 directory trips the existing conformance walk and the majors-equality test because the fixture walker selects *.toml while 026-C3's document is JSON-shaped. Also flagged: 026-S1 has no source ids, since data/manifests/ holds only a README and no manifest.toml exists in the tree. 16 open questions recorded; no files outside the output path were written.
reply.commitMessage: docs: add ADR-026 registry service research
docs: design the ADR-026 root and caching registry service

findings.location: Chosen design → The serving face — "`upstream` is `none` (root) or `ok`/`stale`/`down` (caching)"
findings.problem: 026-C2 closes the health body's `upstream` value to four tokens, and the design makes the verdict a cached gauge that health never probes live ("the verdict is cached and refreshed on the same TTL"), so a caching instance that has not yet contacted its upstream has no legal value to answer: `none` is claimed by root mode, `ok`/`stale` assert a fetch that never happened, and `down` asserts an unreachable upstream never tried. `last_upstream_fetch` also has no defined value before the first fetch, while the design's own `fetched_at` rules refuse non-integers. Test strategy #12 cannot pin the startup body and T-005/T-007 will decide differently; the never-checked state is created by this design's no-live-probe rule.
findings.fix: Name the value for the never-contacted state in the serving-face paragraph (e.g. `upstream: down` with `last_upstream_fetch: 0`) and extend test #12 to pin a freshly started caching instance.

findings.location: Chosen design → The admin face and auth — "`DELETE /v1/admin/games/<game_id>` percent-decodes the path segment, validates the grammar (A4), removes the record."
findings.problem: 026-C4 requires that "every accepted mutation bumps `revision` and persists atomically through the tmp-and-rename discipline", but the design states the bump only for POST and test strategy #10 pins it only for upsert ("upsert validates + bumps `revision` + atomic rename; delete decodes+validates the id"). The Concurrency paragraph's generic "mutations … then write the atomic tmp-and-rename" covers DELETE's persist but not its bump. T-006 can ship a DELETE that leaves `revision` unchanged with every pinned test green, and the Goals promise that mutations are "stated to the level a test engineer can pin" is then false.
findings.fix: Add "bumps `revision` and persists through the same tmp-and-rename" to the DELETE bullet, and "delete bumps `revision` and persists" to test #10.

findings.location: Chosen design → Catalog document and its spec — "The registry's loader (`corpus.rs`) refuses by name: `version != 1`, `revision` negative, a `game_id` failing the grammar+bound (A4) …"
findings.problem: The refusal list is presented as complete and never makes a duplicate `game_id` a refusal, although POST /v1/admin/games is an upsert keyed by game_id and DELETE names one record: a corpus with two records sharing a game_id loads, makes delete ambiguous, makes upsert's whole-record replacement non-deterministic about which row survives the next atomic write, and makes stats' `games` count disagree between loaded model and saved file. The same hole exists in the cache document: 026-C7 sorts entries by slug byte order (one entry per slug implied) while the named cache refusals (test #4: "bad version/shape/`game_id`/`name`") never name a duplicate slug, so a hand-edited cache with two entries for one slug has an undefined TTL winner.
findings.fix: State that corpus.rs refuses a repeated `game_id` (and a repeated `source_key` within one record) and cache.rs refuses a repeated `slug`, by name; add both to the named refusal lists in tests #1 and #4 and to `schemas/catalog/v1/fixtures/invalid/`.

findings.location: Chosen design → CLI amendment — "The two pinned suites (unit + subprocess, A11) re-pin: remote hosts are now admitted" vs Test strategy #15 "**no test dials non-loopback**"
findings.problem: The subprocess suite being re-pinned is endpoint_policy_refuses_everything_beyond_the_loopback_spelling (cli_catalog_gate_tests.rs:112), whose remote cases are http://catalog.example and http://catalog.example:8080/v1 and which asserts today that each fails before enumeration with `catalog transport unavailable`. Once parse_endpoint admits any host those inputs are admitted, so the same subprocess run proceeds into probe() — a DNS lookup of a public domain plus a connect_timeout — producing network-dependent `catalog unreachable` output and violating both #15 and the suite's own invariant (tests/common/mod.rs:12). probe() has no resolver or connector seam, and the amendment names none, so the amendment is either unpinnable or network-dialing.
findings.fix: Pin the split: remote-host admission pinned at parse_endpoint (pure, unit suite; the 026-L2 disclosure line moves there), the subprocess suite keeps only still-refused spellings plus the re-pinned refusal text, and probe()'s admission is pinned only against the in-process loopback fake — or sanction a 192.0.2.1 literal explicitly and correct #15.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets — "The three registry budgets are **private to `apps/registry`** (`constants.rs`)"
findings.problem: Every budget the design names bounds the cache (026-B1/026-B2) or inbound requests; nothing bounds the catalog document — the one document the ADR expects to grow to "tens of thousands of games, each with several store keys". 026-C3 makes the catalog loader's refusals "the schema's, by name, as every contract document's are (`schemas/README.md` discipline)", and that discipline is a size cap that "binds *before* the read" with `schemas/README.md` as "this bound's one stated home" (restated for disk-arriving contract documents in data/manifests/README.md:14-18). corpus.rs therefore reads an arbitrarily large --corpus or local-entries file with no named refusal, no `games` count cap and no cap on `source_keys` per record, and test #1's refusal list has no over-cap case where the cache's does.
findings.fix: Add one private `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` (1_048_576, mirroring 026-B2) checked on file length before the read in corpus.rs, name it in constants.rs and in test #1's refusal list, and state it in schemas/catalog/v1/spec.md as that format's bound.

findings.location: Chosen design → `apps/registry` — one crate, two modes — "It depends on `bindforge-core` for the grammar and name bounds (`is_slug_name`, `MAX_SLUG_OCTETS`, `MAX_NATIVE_NAME_OCTETS`, `escape_and_truncate`)"
findings.problem: The predicate the design leans on hardest is not in core: spells_lookup_key and the closed source-token set are Source's in crates/discovery (A16's own basis; apps/discovery-cli/src/matches.rs:229,282 reaches them via its discovery dependency). The dependency set given (std + serde_json + bindforge-core) cannot serve "a `source_key` failing `spells_lookup_key`" in corpus.rs or "`spells_lookup_key` to it" at /v1/candidates, so T-004/T-005 must either add a dependency the design never lists — pulling the store scanners into the server binary — or re-spell {steam, epic, local} locally, giving the closed set two definitions.
findings.fix: Decide it in the module plan: either "apps/registry depends on `discovery` for `Source`, as discovery-cli already does" in the crate's dependency sentence, or "the closed source-token set and spells_lookup_key are lifted into bindforge-core and Source re-exports them", naming the shipped text each option replaces.

findings.location: Chosen design → The serving face — "The `026-L4` cold case is the named `503` with a legible reason phrase"
findings.problem: That sentence sits in the paragraph both modes share ("The two modes share every handler") and the design never states the root's answer for a well-formed, spellable slug that joins to nothing. 026-L4 confines the 503 to a caching registry with nothing to answer from, and its own reasoning makes [] the true statement for a root that has never heard of the key, so 200 [] is correct — but T-005 reading this section alone can reach 503 or 404, and neither test #2 nor #16 pins it.
findings.fix: Add to serving-face step 2: "an empty join in root mode is a `200` with `[]`; the `503` is reachable only from caching mode", and one case in #16.

findings.location: Chosen design → The admin face and auth — "`GET /v1/admin/stats` answers `{games, source_keys, revision}` from the instance's own catalog document"
findings.problem: The field types are never stated, and 026-L3's no-bulk rule turns on them: an implementer who answers `source_keys` as the list of keys answers with the catalog's whole key set over an admin route — what 026-L3 forbids and what the rejected GET /v1/admin/catalog was rejected for. Test #18 pins only that /v1/admin/catalog is 404.
findings.fix: State that `games` and `source_keys` are integer counts (with `revision`) and pin the three-field count shape in test #10.

findings.location: Chosen design → The admin face and auth — "Enablement is judged from the bind address literal and the presence of a configured token."
findings.problem: The design never says what makes a literal loopback. --host takes the same spelling space the endpoint policy admits (parse_endpoint normalizes hostnames and the amendment widens hosts further), and the shipped precedent judges loopbackness twice and differently: the LOOPBACK_HOSTS literal set for configuration, and addr.ip().is_loopback() on the resolved address in probe(). Under a literal-only rule, `--host localhost` with no token is a coin flip that decides whether the admin face exists — the ADR's own no-token-friction use case.
findings.fix: Judge enablement from the address actually bound (local_addr()'s ip().is_loopback(), the shipped probe() predicate), or name the closed loopback-literal set beside the quoted sentence.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets — "the registry evicts the oldest `fetched_at` until **both** … hold"
findings.problem: Eviction order is the raw wall-clock stamp, while the same paragraph puts TTL on the wall clock "with a guard that treats a backwards-jumped stamp as expired rather than immortal". After a backwards clock jump the entries just fetched are the "oldest", so the dual-cap eviction discards the freshest data first and repeatedly, and re-fetched answers are evicted again while stale entries remain serviceable.
findings.fix: Order eviction by a monotonic insert sequence held beside `fetched_at` (insertion order, ties broken by `fetched_at`) and say so in test #5 instead of "oldest `fetched_at` evicted first".

findings.location: Risks — "Two `registry serve` on one corpus fail loudly" row — "State it as a refused, unsupported configuration in `spec.md` and the CLI's startup check."
findings.problem: The mechanism relied on is the fixed-name create_new(true) tmp, which fails only at save time: a second instance starts, loads the corpus and serves reads indefinitely, and a tmp left by a crash is indistinguishable from a live writer's. No module in the nine-file plan owns an instance marker, so the promised startup check has no mechanism and no test (#11 pins only "a second save over a stale tmp fails loudly").
findings.fix: Drop "and the CLI's startup check", leaving the loud write-time failure as the contract answer, or name the marker (an exclusive-create registry.lock beside the corpus, taken at startup) as an apps/registry behavior with its own case in #11.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets — "`MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS` (a POST body cap)"
findings.problem: Of the two new private request budgets only one is given a value (MAX_REQUEST_HEADER_OCTETS, 65,536), so the refusal test #11 pins has no boundary to sit on, and it interacts with the uncapped `source_keys` array: a record legal under 026-C3 can outgrow any number the implementer picks. Inbound framing is unstated with it: the response writer's Transfer-Encoding ban is pinned, but nothing says how a chunked or Content-Length-less admin POST is answered.
findings.fix: State the number with the record bound it is sized against, and add to http.rs: a request body without a decimal Content-Length, or over the cap, is refused before any mutation.

findings.location: Options considered — "the two shipped JSON documents (`matches.json`, the candidate body) already live *outside* the TOML formats contract (A5, A6)"; Chosen design → Budgets — "its private `STORE_READ_BUDGET_OCTETS` (A7)"
findings.problem: The anchors do not carry the facts. A5 is the MAX_NATIVE_NAME_OCTETS bound and A6 the data-directory rule; neither states that those documents sit outside the TOML subset (that is conformance.rs's .toml fixture walk plus matches.rs's serde_json store). A7 is the atomic-persist row; the over-budget file refusal is STORE_READ_BUDGET_OCTETS at matches.rs:36,194, which no register row covers — and it is also the load-bearing precedent for the cache and catalog load refusals.
findings.fix: Add one register row for matches.rs's private read-budget refusal (`load`, STORE_READ_BUDGET_OCTETS) and re-anchor both passages to it.

findings.location: Deferred / out of scope — "The seed corpus adopting the real shipped manifest ids once the first manifest PR lands (`data/manifests/` is empty, A14)"
findings.problem: This deferral contradicts its source clause rather than merely deferring it: 026-S1 requires a corpus "opened with a handful of real games (game ids drawn from the shipped manifest ids…)". The empty manifest tree makes the clause unsatisfiable today (A14 verified: data/manifests/README.md:10), so minting provisional ids is the only possible act — but Rollout step 6's ledger annotations name only 025-C4, 025-L1 and 025-R1, so the ledger will record 026-S1 as discharged by a corpus that does not satisfy it.
findings.fix: Add 026-S1 to Rollout step 6's annotations (an amended-by / partially-satisfied-by line per 021-L4 recording that the seed mints grammar-valid ids while data/manifests/ is empty), so the divergence is visible on the unit itself.

findings.location: Chosen design → The serving face — "mode is an enum field on the server state, so a client cannot tell which answered (`026-C1`)"
findings.problem: The same face's GET /v1/health answers `mode` and `upstream` by name, and a caching instance's cold 503 where root answers 200 [] is a mode-revealing difference the ADR itself mandates, so the claim as written is false.
findings.fix: Scope it: "GET /v1/candidates is byte-identical between modes; health reports `mode` by design."

findings.location: Chosen design → CLI amendment — "**drops the `LOOPBACK_HOSTS` host check**"
findings.problem: Retiring the check leaves const LOOPBACK_HOSTS (catalog.rs:34) unused, and the repo gate is `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`. The Goals line ("retirement named at all three shipped sites") covers it in spirit but the amendment's bullet list does not.
findings.fix: Name the constant's deletion in the first bullet.

findings.location: Revision log — "(§\"Where the format contract and the ADR disagree\", open Q1/Q2)" and "(§Platform notes, open Q7)"
findings.problem: Both entries anchor to sections this document does not have; the decisions now live in "Catalog document and its spec" and "The serving face", so the log's pointers cannot be followed by a reviser.
findings.fix: Re-point both entries at the sections that now hold the decision.

findings.location: Compatibility matrix — "Other / exotic Unix (BSD et al.) | unknown | Treated by the Unix data-dir branch; `std::net` assumed portable; not exercised by any suite here."
findings.problem: The compatibility checklist requires every platform row to carry a status, and `unknown` is not a status but the absence of a decision. The matrix footer makes the gap load-bearing ("the matrix describes the target `apps/registry` behavior the tasks must meet"), so `T-004`…`T-008` inherit no promise and no refusal for a row the matrix simultaneously says is handled by the shipped Unix data-dir branch; CI never exercises it, so nothing can establish its behavior. The cell is populated, so this is major rather than a blocker.
findings.fix: Replace that row's status `unknown` with the decision `No` and rewrite its Notes to "not a v1 target: the Unix data-dir branch and `std::net` may carry it, nothing exercises or promises it", and extend the matrix footer from "the matrix describes the target `apps/registry` behavior the tasks must meet" to name the three `Yes` rows (Linux/Unix CI, macOS, Windows) as the rows the tasks owe behavior to. Text replacement only; Test strategy #19 needs no change because the row becomes unsupported rather than supported.

findings.location: Catalog document and its spec + Test strategy #1 — "`schemas/catalog/v1/` ships `spec.md` + `fixtures/valid/*.json` + `fixtures/invalid/*.json`"
findings.problem: The shipped JSON fixtures are counted by the harness and parsed by nothing: every named harness edit skips them ("guard `every_valid_fixture_…`, `every_invalid_fixture_…` and the single-line/truncation loops behind the core-TOML check"), the zero-fixture rule only tests directory emptiness (verified in `crates/core/tests/common/mod.rs::zero_fixture_violation`), and Test strategy #1's loader case states its faults without naming the fixtures as its inputs. `026-C3`'s "Loader refusals are the schema's, by name" is then unpinned for the new format, and third-party readers get a corpus no suite proves, since the TOML walk that has always been the formats contract's language-neutral half now excludes the directory.
findings.fix: Re-word Test strategy #1's inputs to the shipped corpus — "a valid corpus loads" becomes "every `fixtures/valid/*.json` loads, and each of … is a named refusal at `fixtures/invalid/*.json`" — and add one clause to the `crates/core/tests/common/mod.rs` bullet recording that the JSON fixture directories stay under the existing fixture-name and case-uniqueness rule (`fixture_file_names_are_lowercase_ascii_dash_separated_and_case_unique`, which walks every `format_dirs()` entry) now that `is_fixture_name` accepts `.json` for external formats. Points existing suites at existing files; adds no mechanism.

findings.location: Chosen design → Serving face — "Percent-decode `slug` **first**, then apply `025-B1`'s 128-octet cap to the *decoded* bytes and `spells_lookup_key` to it; the corpus/index is keyed by the decoded string" (same predicate at "Catalog document and its spec": "a `source_key` failing `spells_lookup_key` or `025-B1`"; cache-load refusal list omits `slug`)
findings.problem: The admitted lookup-key spelling is too weak for the network-fed seams: `spells_lookup_key` (crates/discovery/src/game.rs) is shape-only — closed source token, one `/`, non-empty external-id, no character or dot rule — and `025-B1` is a length cap, so `slug=local/%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fetc%2fpasswd` decodes to `local/../../etc/passwd` and passes the design's own admission gate for `/v1/candidates`, passes the admin upsert, and is persistable into the corpus and cache documents (whose load refusals name `game_id`/`name` but never `slug`). The design never pins which spellings are accepted nor states the key's data plane, so the property "dot- and separator-bearing keys can never ask the filesystem for a path" cannot be established from the text, while the codebase's own precedent (`is_slug_name`'s doc: the grammar exists so `..`/separators never "ask the filesystem for a path") makes a path-joined index the pattern a T-005/T-007 implementer reaches for (security checklist 3).
findings.fix: Pin the admitted spelling — after the first `/`, exactly one non-empty `.`-free component with no embedded `/` — as one named validator applied at the candidate query, the admin upsert, and cache load (adding `slug` to the named cache refusals), and state that lookup keys are opaque in-memory strings that are never joined onto paths, replacing the bare `spells_lookup_key`-plus-length gate at those three seams.

findings.location: Chosen design → apps/registry module plan — "`serve.rs` — accept loop (one thread per connection, request-read timeout to bound low-and-slow)" (with §Risks row "Low-and-slow / one-inbound-per-outbound exposure on a routable bind")
findings.problem: For a publicly reachable root with an anonymous serving face, the pinned defenses bound inbound bytes only: no cap on concurrently open connections (one OS thread each, held to the read timeout or longer), and the named timeout is a read timeout — a peer that never reads the response parks a writer thread indefinitely, so unauthenticated connection buildup can exhaust the process.
findings.fix: Name `MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS` in `constants.rs` with an immediate close when over the cap, and a write-side timeout or overall per-connection deadline, in the `serve.rs` line and that risk row's mitigation.

findings.location: Chosen design → The admin face and auth — "`--admin-token` or `BINDFORGE_REGISTRY_ADMIN_TOKEN`" (cf. Caching mode's "dropped with one escaped, single-line echo")
findings.problem: The design states the escaping posture for echoed untrusted ids but never states the logging posture for the admin token: nothing says the configured token never enters refusal lines, logs, health/stats output, or the `401` path's text; `026-R1` carries transport assurance, not local/accidental disclosure.
findings.fix: Add one sentence to the admin section: the configured token is never echoed by any refusal, log line, or status surface; `401` responses carry only `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` and the status line.

findings.location: Chosen design → Catalog document and its spec — "Nothing on disk is rewritten on refusal (A7's load discipline)" (seed corpus loaded by `corpus.rs` from `data/catalog/v1/catalog.json`)
findings.problem: The corpus is the one document the design loads with no read budget: the cache gets `026-B2` re-checked at load and the match-store precedent caps its read at `STORE_READ_BUDGET_OCTETS` before parsing, but the corpus is checked only by per-record bounds known after the parse, so an oversized or corrupt corpus parses unbounded.
findings.fix: Mirror the precedent: a private corpus-read byte budget checked on file metadata before the parse, stated in `corpus.rs`'s line.

findings.location: Chosen design → Caching mode — "It **refuses redirects** (a `3xx` is an upstream error → `stale`/`503`)"
findings.problem: The framing-mirror discipline (reject `Transfer-Encoding`, duplicated/non-decimal `Content-Length`) is pinned only for responses the registry reads; the inbound request reader's framing is left open, and the `026-R1` deployment posture (an edge terminating TLS in front of the root) makes a CL/TE mismatch between that edge and the hand-written reader a request-smuggling seam.
findings.fix: Extend the mirror sentence to `http.rs`'s request reader: inbound bodies are `Content-Length`-framed only; a request `Transfer-Encoding` is a named refusal.

findings.location: Caching mode, lookup step 4 ("Miss with reachable upstream fetches `GET <upstream>/v1/candidates?slug=`, validates the answer, and caches it with its `fetched_at`") together with Chosen design → Budgets ("after any cache write, the registry evicts the oldest `fetched_at` until **both** `count ≤ 026-B1` **and** `serialized bytes ≤ 026-B2` hold — so the file is provably inside both caps after every mutation")
findings.problem: The per-lookup cost on the request path is unbudgeted and unbounded in work. Each cold lookup must (a) serialize the whole cache document to test the byte invariant, (b) re-sort entries by `slug` byte order for the next write per `026-C7`, (c) find the oldest `fetched_at` among up to 5,000 entries, and (d) re-persist the entire document through the `026-C7`/A7 tmp-write + rename + re-chmod discipline — up to 1,048,576 octets rewritten per slug, synchronously, in the handler. The shipped client's scan is a serial per-slug loop (apps/discovery-cli/src/main.rs:191-192, `for slug in &unresolved { catalog.candidates(slug) … }`) and `026-R3` keeps prefetch deferred, so a first scan of N games pays N × (serialize + sort + evict scan + full-file rewrite) of a document growing toward `026-B2`: O(N × cache bytes) on the user-visible critical path on top of the N serial upstream round trips. No request-latency budget appears anywhere in the document; the Risks row for the cold-scan cliff mitigates only the extra health round trip ("Cache the upstream-health verdict and reuse lookup outcome"), and the low-and-slow row's "oldest-first cache eviction bounds the entry growth" bounds entry count, not per-write work.
findings.fix: Keep the dual invariant but make it incremental: hold each entry's serialized octet count in the in-memory cache model with a running total, so the post-write check is O(1) plus evictions rather than a whole-document re-serialization, replacing the currently implied per-mutation serialization; and state in one sentence when the cache file is rewritten (write-through per lookup, or coalesced at end-of-scan/idle plus clean shutdown with the crash-loss window named). Add the matching assertion to Test-strategy #5.

findings.location: Chosen design → Catalog document and its spec ("The registry's loader (`corpus.rs`) refuses by name: `version != 1`, `revision` negative, a `game_id` failing the grammar+bound (A4), a `name` over 128 octets (A5), a `source_key` failing `spells_lookup_key` or `025-B1` (A3, A16), a non-object/missing field") and §Budgets
findings.problem: The `026-C3` catalog document is the only document this design loads with no octet ceiling and no entry-count cap, while every other load is budgeted (cache at `026-B2` = 1,048,576; the newly elaborated `MAX_REQUEST_HEADER_OCTETS`/`MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS`). All listed refusals are field-level. The A7 load discipline the section cites as its model includes a size gate: matches.rs refuses "past the 65536-octet read budget" on `fs::metadata` before allocating (apps/discovery-cli/src/matches.rs:36,194) and core refuses over `MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES` "without being allocated" (crates/core/src/toml.rs:56). So the root's boot read, its retained in-memory model, and the slug→candidates index — the design's main translation table — are unbounded against the ADR's own sizing ("tens of thousands of games, each with several store keys"), and in caching mode the admin face can grow the local-entries document without limit.
findings.fix: Add one private constant in `constants.rs` (`MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS`, following the `STORE_READ_BUDGET_OCTETS` precedent the design already invokes: an `fs::metadata` gate before the read), refused by name at load for both the `--corpus` file and the local-entries document; list it beside the other private budgets in §Budgets and add a refusal case to Test-strategy #1. No new ADR unit is needed, since §Budgets already justifies private request-side budgets as `026-C2`/`026-C4` elaboration.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets ("The research's \"budgets do not close\" finding (5,000 entries × up to 256 candidates can exceed 1 MiB) is resolved by making both caps **write-time** invariants")
findings.problem: The resolution makes `026-B1`'s 5,000 nominal but states no resulting effective capacity, which the numbers put far lower. Each entry's candidates arrive in a response capped at `MAX_RESPONSE_OCTETS = 65_536` with ≤ 256 `{game_id, name}` pairs (game_id ≤ 128, name ≤ 128: crates/core/src/placement.rs:83, crates/core/src/manifest.rs:58), so one saturated entry is ≈64 KiB and `026-B2` alone caps the cache at ≈16 slugs; at a realistic ~40-octet candidate it is ≈90. With oldest-first eviction, a few fat entries evict many thin ones, so the working set may be tens of slugs rather than 5,000 — deepening the cold-scan cliff the design itself flags (`026-R3`). The r0 revision entry made the caps jointly satisfiable, which is sound, but supplies no capacity number for T-007's eviction test or for reading `health.cached_slugs`.
findings.fix: One sentence in §Budgets giving the per-entry worst case derived from `MAX_RESPONSE_OCTETS` and the resulting effective slug capacity, stated as accepted, so the eviction unit test and operator-facing counts are pinned to the right expectation.

findings.location: Chosen design → The admin face and auth, "Concurrency (open Q10)" ("serving reads take the lock on the **in-memory** model (never the file)" / "mutations take the same lock, mutate the model, then write the atomic tmp-and-rename")
findings.problem: As written every `GET /v1/candidates` takes an exclusive `Mutex<Corpus>`, so candidate queries serialize against each other even with no writer, and the tmp-write + rename + re-chmod — synchronous filesystem IO on a document the ADR sizes in the tens of thousands of entries — happens inside that same lock, so one admin POST/DELETE stalls the whole serving face for the duration of the disk write. This bears on the design's flagship deployment (a public root on a routable bind per `026-C5`) with thread-per-connection serving. The mutex is only load-bearing for the two-writer refusal, which is already enforced by the fixed-name `create_new(true)` tmp (A7).
findings.fix: Name the primitive and the persist's placement in one sentence: `Arc<RwLock<Corpus>>` with reads on the shared lock, and the tmp-and-rename either stated as held under the write lock with a stated cost expectation, or performed under a separate persist lock so the serving path never waits on the filesystem.

findings.location: Risks row "Low-and-slow / one-inbound-per-outbound exposure on a routable bind" ("Thread-per-connection with a request-read timeout; `MAX_REQUEST_HEADER_OCTETS`/`MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS`; oldest-first cache eviction bounds the entry growth (`026-B1`)")
findings.problem: The mitigations bound bytes and time per connection but nothing bounds the number of connections, and the model allocates one OS thread per connection under the `std`-only posture with no runtime to absorb it. A peer holding many idle keep-alive sockets on a non-loopback bind drives unbounded thread/stack growth. The cited "entry growth" bound covers cache entries (`026-B1`), not connections, so the row claims coverage it does not provide.
findings.fix: Add one more private constant to the §Budgets `constants.rs` list (`MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS`, excess refused at accept, or a stated accept-backlog posture) and replace the cache-eviction clause in that mitigation with it; pin it in Test-strategy #11.

findings.location: Caching mode, "Upstream reachability" ("that verdict is **cached and refreshed on the same TTL**") read against Serving face ("it does not perform a live upstream probe per call")
findings.problem: The design never names what performs the TTL refresh. Lookup steps 1-2 (local entry, warm cache) make zero upstream requests, so `health.upstream` can go arbitrarily long without an upstream interaction, and the module plan (`serve.rs` accept loop/router/mode selection, `upstream.rs` client) names no timer or refresher. If the refresh is lazy inside `GET /v1/health`, the route the design says never probes does issue one at every TTL boundary, and a monitoring poller pays the mirrored 2 s connect / 5 s read timeout inside a health check — with `--refresh-interval` free to make that boundary frequent.
findings.fix: One sentence naming the driver: a background refresher on the TTL interval owned by `serve.rs` (which also makes "last-known" literally true), or an explicit statement that the health route may pay at most one bounded upstream probe per TTL, with that probe's timeout pinned.

findings.location: Chosen design → The serving face, join step 2 ("Answer = the join: games whose `source_keys` contain the slug")
findings.problem: This is the design's only statement of the hot-path algorithm and it describes a linear scan over every game and its `source_keys` per request. The structure that avoids it appears only in the module list (`corpus.rs` — "load + validate + the slug→candidates index") and is never connected to the route or to the stable-ordering requirement, so as written a request scans and sorts before "Ordered by `game_id` byte order; truncated to the first `MAX_CANDIDATES`".
findings.fix: State in step 2 that the slug→candidates index maps the decoded slug to postings already sorted by `game_id` byte order at load, so a request is a probe plus a clone of at most `MAX_CANDIDATES` projected records, and that sort and truncation cost is paid at load, not per request.

findings.location: §Options considered ("the harness carve-out is the honest cost, not the format choice") + §The seed corpus + §Catalog document and its spec ("`schemas/catalog/v1/` ships `spec.md` + `fixtures/valid/*.json`")
findings.problem: The JSON-carve-out file list names only crates/core/tests changes and misses a second shipped consumer of the same trees: crates/discovery/tests/boundary_tests.rs::the_shipped_corpus_carries_no_source_key_spelling walks every file under data/ recursively plus every schemas/*/v*/fixtures/valid/ (walk_files recurses) and fails if any contains the literal `steam/`, `epic/` or `local/`. Since Source::spells_lookup_key (crates/discovery/src/game.rs:84) admits only those three tokens, no valid catalog document can live under those trees: the 026-S1 seed "each carrying its `steam/<appid>` source_key" and every valid schemas/catalog/v1/fixtures/valid/*.json both trip it, so T-004 as scoped cannot pass `cargo test --workspace --locked`. The options comparison also priced the choice on an incomplete cost: the sweep covers data/ as well, so the rejected "just don't put it in schemas/" alternative would not have avoided it either.
findings.fix: Add the amendment to that same bullet list: re-scope that sweep to data/manifests and data/profiles (or exempt data/catalog/ and schemas/catalog/v1/fixtures/), re-pin its doc-comment and its `checked > 0` guard, and restate the Options paragraph naming both harness consumers. 026-S1 mandates the keys, so the sweep moves, not the seed.

findings.location: §`apps/registry` — one crate, two modes ("It depends on `bindforge-core` for the grammar and name bounds") + §Caching mode ("reuses the shipped client's response discipline with its own private constants") + §CLI amendment ("mirroring `parse_endpoint`") + §Deferred ("pinned by the same `StoreLayout` env-closure seam")
findings.problem: The reuse language describes sharing the crate layout cannot provide: apps/discovery-cli is a bin-only crate (its Cargo.toml declares no [lib]; apps/ holds only src/main.rs, src/catalog.rs, src/matches.rs), so the response reader and count caps, parse_endpoint, game_id_is_valid (matches.rs:354), StoreLayout/data_dir/store_path (matches.rs:46-103) and the tmp-and-rename save/owner_only_new_file discipline are unreachable from apps/registry — the design ships a second copy of five shipped invariants and defers the lift for exactly one of them. Meanwhile the one validator that is importable, Source::spells_lookup_key, lives in crates/discovery, a dependency the dependency sentence never names, so Test strategy #8's "runs through `game_id_is_valid`" names a function in another crate's binary.
findings.fix: In §Chosen design replace "reuses"/"mirroring"/"the same … seam" with one short shared-vs-copied list naming, per block (response discipline, endpoint gate, game_id predicate, <data> rule, atomic persist, source-key spelling), whether the task lifts it to a shared crate (bindforge-core or a small new one) or duplicates it plus a pinning test; and state the real dependency line for apps/registry (bindforge-core + discovery + serde_json). Smaller design: lift the three store/IO blocks once so both binaries call the same code, which also removes the duplicated env-closure seam Test #13 and the Compatibility matrix rely on.

findings.location: §Budgets ("`MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS` (a POST body cap)") and the same section's ("a `fetched_at` that is not a non-negative integer within a plausible-clock bound")
findings.problem: Two of the design's own refusal thresholds are named without a value, while Test strategy #11 ("MAX_REQUEST_HEADER_OCTETS/MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS refusals") and #4 ("a `fetched_at` outside the load bound is refused") pin behavior against them. A section whose stated goal is that the budgets close against each other cannot establish that for an unvalued cap, and the task author must invent the number the proposal exists to decide.
findings.fix: State both numbers in the same sentence (e.g. body cap = 65_536 mirroring the header cap; fetched_at accepted within [now − horizon, now + skew] with both named) and cite them from #4/#11 by value, not by constant name alone.

findings.location: §Caching mode ("Upstream **reachability** (the `health.upstream` gauge) is gauged by the upstream's own `/v1/health`, but that verdict is **cached and refreshed on the same TTL**")
findings.problem: No trigger is named for that refresh, and the module plan (main/serve/http/corpus/admin/cache/upstream/endpoint/constants, serve.rs = "accept loop (one thread per connection…)") has no scheduler. Either the /v1/health probe never runs, leaving health.upstream derived only from lookup outcomes and not honoring the 026-C6 clause the section cites, or a background timer arrives as an unplanned tenth moving part. The same paragraph's claim that "A cold query therefore does not pay a separate upstream health round trip" only holds while the verdict is unexpired.
findings.fix: One sentence naming the trigger — the probe runs at most once per TTL, fired lazily by the first lookup after expiry on that request's own thread, with no timer thread — and reword the round-trip claim as "no additional health round trip per query beyond the one TTL-gated probe".

findings.location: §CLI surface ("overridable by `--local-entries <path>`", "`--refresh-interval` overrides `026-B3`")
findings.problem: Neither knob has a consumer anywhere in the Test strategy: #14 pins only --upstream, #16 passes --corpus, #13 reaches the paths through the env seam, and no item starts a caching instance with a relocated entries document or a shortened TTL. --refresh-interval is 026-B3-mandated and --local-entries is invented beyond 026-C1's flag list, so the design pays for two knobs it never exercises.
findings.fix: Add one clause to #6 or #17 per knob — a TTL override that expires a cached entry early, and a caching run with --local-entries on a scratch path proving the admin mutation lands there — or drop --local-entries and let the tests relocate via HOME/XDG_DATA_HOME as #13 already does.

findings.location: §Catalog document and its spec ("guard `every_valid_fixture_…`, `every_invalid_fixture_…` and the single-line/truncation loops behind the core-TOML check")
findings.problem: Of the loops named, only every_valid_fixture_re_serializes_to_a_semantically_equal_value, every_invalid_fixture_is_rejected_with_a_structured_error and every_invalid_fixture_is_rejected_with_a_single_line_message walk the fixture tree; the truncation case (a_rejection_truncates_an_untrusted_value_rather_than_echoing_it) parses a hand-built document, so guarding it adds a dead conditional. The list also omits the call site the .json rule actually needs: fixture_file_names_are_lowercase_ascii_dash_separated_and_case_unique asserts is_fixture_name(name) for every file in the tree, and is_fixture_name takes a bare name with no format argument.
findings.fix: Name the three walking loops plus the fixture-name test, drop "truncation", and say whether is_fixture_name gains a format argument or the call site is guarded.

findings.location: §Catalog document and its spec ("recognize a small `EXTERNAL_JSON_FORMATS = ["catalog"]` set") + §Risks ("pin it with a test that the list is the single source")
findings.problem: A general external-format registry plus a meta-test about the list's own use, built for exactly one member — an abstraction layer with one implementation.
findings.fix: Use one const naming `catalog` at the skip site with the schemas/README.md paragraph as the record, and generalize when a second JSON format actually arrives; keep as written only if the panel wants the forward-compat on the record.

reply.summary: Round 1 consumed all 10 majors: the never-contacted `upstream: down`/`last_upstream_fetch: 0` startup body plus #12 pin; DELETE's revision-bump/persist plus #10; repeated `game_id`/`slug` named refusals (#1, #4, fixtures); CLI suite split so remote admission is pinned only at `parse_endpoint` in the unit suite (#15); `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` metadata-gated before read, stated in spec.md (correctness+performance duplicate consolidated); real dependency line `bindforge-core`+`discovery`+`serde_json` with the five bin-only-copied invariants listed once and their lift deferred (replacing the data-dir-only deferral); exotic-Unix matrix row decided `No` with footer naming the three Yes rows; a single tightened lookup-key validator governing candidate query, upsert, and cache load with keys declared path-opaque; incremental write-time dual-cap accounting with insertion-order eviction, write-through persist, and the accepted ≈16-fat-entry working set; and the `boundary_tests` source-key sweep re-scope with the Options cost restated. Most minors/nits folded in (root `200 []`, integer stats, bound-address enablement, valued body cap, connection cap and inbound framing, token-echo ban, lazy TTL probe driver, load-sorted index, A22 register row, 026-S1 ledger annotation, deleted `--local-entries` knob, dropped startup-check claim, scoped byte-identity claim, retitled revision anchors). Diff is net positive because five findings each required a named new mechanism (validator, two constants, harness amendment, suite split, startup body) that deletion or deferral could not close; the revision log supersedes seven r0 entries in place and adds five.
reply.commitMessage: docs: revise 026 registry proposal for round-1 design panel findings

findings.location: Chosen design → The admin face and auth, Concurrency — "mutations take the write lock, mutate the model, and perform the atomic tmp-and-rename under a separate persist-only lock, so serving reads never wait on filesystem IO"
findings.problem: The r1 revision made this sentence either self-refuting or silently unsound, with no pinned case on either horn. If the tmp-and-rename happens while the model write lock is still held (the literal reading of the clause chain), serving reads wait on filesystem IO, which is exactly what the clause promises they never do. If the write lock is released before the persist, the text states neither when the snapshot is taken nor how persists are ordered with mutations, so two accepted admin mutations can persist newest-first and leave the file holding the older revision's record set while memory holds the newer one: after a restart an accepted mutation is gone and `revision` runs backwards, which 026-C4 forbids ("every accepted mutation bumps `revision` and persists atomically"). Test #11 pins only "a reader never sees a torn document (served from the locked in-memory model)" and #10 pins one upsert and one delete, so T-006 ships either horn with every pinned test green.
findings.fix: State the lock order and the snapshot point in one clause replacing "mutate the model, and perform the atomic tmp-and-rename under a separate persist-only lock": "the persist lock is taken before the model write lock; the mutation serializes the model into bytes while still holding both, releases the model lock, then does the tmp-and-rename under the persist lock alone"; and add to #11: N concurrent mutations ⇒ after all return, the file equals the model and `revision` equals the final value.

findings.location: Compatibility matrix — "Linux & other Unix | Yes" vs "Other / exotic Unix (BSD et al.) | No"
findings.problem: The r1 edit flipped the fourth row from `unknown` to `No` without touching row 1's label, so the matrix now says other Unix is both supported and not supported; the closing sentence ("the three `Yes` rows (Linux & other-Unix CI, macOS, Windows)") compounds the contradiction.
findings.fix: Relabel row 1 "Linux (primary CI target)" and let row 4 carry the `No`, or state that row 1's "other Unix" names only the shared Unix data-dir branch, not a support promise.

findings.location: Chosen design → Caching mode, Upstream reachability — "probed **at most once per TTL**, fired lazily by the first lookup or health read after expiry on that request's own thread"
findings.problem: This contradicts the serving face's "Answering it reads the last-known upstream verdict … it does not perform a live upstream probe per call": a health read after TTL expiry now runs a synchronous upstream round trip (up to the 2 s/5 s timeouts) on the health request's own thread. And because `last_upstream_fetch: 0` is expired from the first instant, the new #12 pin ("a freshly started caching instance answers `upstream: down`, `last_upstream_fetch: 0`") is order-dependent — an implementer who applies the probe's verdict before writing the response fails exactly that case whenever the upstream is reachable.
findings.fix: "A health read never fires the probe; only lookups do" (or "health answers from the verdict as it stood at entry and fires the probe after the response is written"), and say so in #12.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets — "evicts the oldest entry by **insertion sequence** (ties by `fetched_at` …)"
findings.problem: The r1 eviction-order fix changed the eviction key away from 026-B1's own words ("over the cap the oldest `fetched_at` is evicted") and records the divergence nowhere, while the design carefully records far smaller ones (`026-S1` in Rollout step 6, the 026-L1/T-008 window in step 5). Test #5 now pins "oldest insertion sequence evicted first", and #5 is the text handed to T-007.
findings.fix: Add one clause — "which equals `026-B1`'s oldest-`fetched_at` order except across a backwards clock jump, where the ADR's rule would evict fresh data" — and add `026-B1` to Rollout step 6's annotations per `021-L4`; also state whether a refreshed entry keeps or takes a new insertion sequence.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets — "`MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` (1,048,576), `fs::metadata`-gated before the read of the `--corpus` or local-entries file, refused by name"
findings.problem: At a realistic ~120-140 octets per `{game_id, name, source_keys}` record, 1 MiB holds roughly 7,500 records — an order of magnitude below the ADR's stated corpus ("tens of thousands of games, each with several store keys", Context) — so the newly named refusal fires on the root's own corpus long before the scale the ADR names as the reason for the design. My r1 fix proposed mirroring 026-B2; the design's adoption makes that number load-bearing for the corpus, where in the ADR it bounded a cache.
findings.fix: Size the cap from the ADR's stated scale and show the arithmetic in `schemas/catalog/v1/spec.md` (e.g. 16 MiB ≈ 120k records), or state explicitly that a corpus past the cap is out of contract for v1 and what its operator does instead.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets — "`MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS` (65,536, sized to one `026-C3` record inside the document cap)"
findings.problem: There is no per-record size to size against: 026-C3 bounds each `source_key` by 025-B1 and never bounds how many a record carries, so the largest legal record is unbounded and the sizing claim cannot be satisfied. The two faces of one document then disagree — `corpus.rs` loads a record carrying 600 keys from disk while `POST /v1/admin/games` refuses the same record as over-cap — and no pinned test sits on that seam.
findings.fix: Either set the body cap to the document cap ("any record that could legally live in a loadable corpus fits, so no per-record key-count bound is needed"), or name `MAX_SOURCE_KEYS_PER_RECORD` in `constants.rs` with a refusal in `corpus.rs`, `admin.rs` and #1, and state the record arithmetic behind the 65,536 figure.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets — "`MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS` (over-cap closed at accept, one thread per admitted connection)"
findings.problem: This is the only budget in the section without a value, so #11's "over-`MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS` is closed at accept" has no boundary to sit on; and a bare close is the one inbound refusal in the design that is not named, where every other refusal is (the client's own outcome is `transport unavailable`/unreachable rather than a stated answer).
findings.fix: Give the number with the thread story it prices, and state the over-cap answer ("closed without a status line; the CLI reports its named unreachable") or a `503` with a reason phrase, which A21 already treats as temporary.

findings.location: Chosen design → The serving face step 1 — "the registry's one key validator tightens it: after the first `/`, exactly one non-empty `.`-free component, no embedded `/`"
findings.problem: The validator is stated only by two exclusions, so everything else is admitted: percent-decoded control bytes (`%0a%0d`, `%00`), spaces and non-UTF-8 become legal keys in the cache document, in the corpus via admin upsert, and in any refusal that names the key (the cold answer is written as `HTTP/1.1 503 No catalog answer for slug`; the design's single-line escaping discipline is stated only for the failed upstream id). Conversely the flat `.`-ban refuses the very keys the ADR names as the point of the admin face — Context: "a `local/<dir>` install has a lookup key" — and directory names carry dots routinely, while the stated purpose (never let a `..` or separator reach a path) needs no more than banning a `.`/`..` component and further separators.
findings.fix: State the accepted key grammar positively: either name the byte set (`[a-z0-9-]` per component, `is_slug_name` as the cited precedent, plus "a decoded key that is invalid UTF-8 or carries a control byte is the `404`"), or keep the path-safety purpose honest ("a component equal to `.` or `..`, or any further `/`, is the `404`") and say whether a `.`-bearing external id is in contract for v1; extend #3 to pin the byte-set answer.

findings.location: Chosen design → Catalog document and its spec — "a repeated `game_id` (records are keyed by it, so a duplicate loads ambiguously)"
findings.problem: The r1 fix was taken halfway: a repeated `source_key` within one record is still not a refusal, so a record may carry `steam/730` twice, which the `corpus.rs` slug→candidates index turns into duplicate `{game_id, name}` postings (the same game twice inside `MAX_CANDIDATES`, crowding out other answers), and `stats`' `source_keys` count becomes ambiguous between total and distinct — the count shape #10 now pins.
findings.fix: Add "a repeated `source_key` within one record" to the `corpus.rs` refusal list and to #1's `fixtures/invalid/` roster.

findings.location: Chosen design → Catalog document and its spec, harness list — "guard the fixture-tree loops — … and `fixture_file_names_…` (which keeps governing the `.json` fixtures: lowercase dash-separated names, case-unique) — behind the core-TOML check so catalog fixtures are not parsed as TOML"
findings.problem: The two halves cancel: a loop guarded behind the core-TOML check by definition stops governing catalog's fixtures, and #19's Windows/macOS case-collision argument rests on that very test covering them. Verified also that shipped `is_fixture_name` takes a bare name (`crates/core/tests/common/mod.rs:421`, one call site at `conformance.rs:348`), so "accepts `.json` for that directory only" is a signature change, not a predicate tweak.
findings.fix: Split the bullet: the re-serialization and both `every_invalid_fixture_…` message loops skip `catalog`; `fixture_file_names_are_lowercase_ascii_dash_separated_and_case_unique` keeps running over it, with the dir-aware `is_fixture_name` named at its one call site.

findings.location: Chosen design → Catalog document and its spec, harness list — "re-scope the sweep to `data/manifests` + `data/profiles`" (with the Risks row "Single `const` names `catalog` at the skip sites; the re-scoped `boundary_tests` sweep … keeps the hygiene gate where it belongs")
findings.problem: Verified at `crates/discovery/tests/boundary_tests.rs:116-130`: the sweep walks every `schemas/*/v*/fixtures/valid/` today, so the re-scope deletes the gate's hold on every other format's valid fixtures — a future `steam/`-bearing `schemas/profiles/…/valid/*.toml` passes green. And the mitigation's single `const` cannot span the two harnesses it names: `crates/core/tests/common/mod.rs` is not reachable from `crates/discovery/tests/boundary_tests.rs` (separate crates, separate test binaries).
findings.fix: Keep the sweep whole and exclude only the catalog format's own directories — a small local exclusion list in `boundary_tests.rs`, the `const` staying at core's skip sites — instead of narrowing the sweep to two `data/` subdirs.

findings.location: Options considered — "the rejected location dodges neither harness consumer — the conformance walk nor the `data/`-walking source-key sweep"
findings.problem: The reasoning is inverted for the first half: moving the format spec out of `schemas/` dodges the conformance walk entirely, which is A9's whole point; only the `data/`-walking sweep survives, because 026-S1 fixes the seed path whatever the spec's location is.
findings.fix: "The rejected location dodges only the conformance walk — the seed at `data/catalog/v1/` still trips the `data/`-walking sweep, and `026-C3` fixes the spec path anyway."

findings.location: Chosen design → The admin face and auth — "Enablement is judged from the address actually bound — the shipped `probe()` predicate `local_addr().ip().is_loopback()`, not a literal-spelling comparison"
findings.problem: That call is not shipped: `probe()`'s predicate is `addr.ip().is_loopback()` on a resolved outbound address (apps/discovery-cli/src/catalog.rs:248) and `local_addr` appears nowhere in the codebase; the same design deletes that shipped refusal at T-008, so "the shipped `probe()` predicate" points an implementer at a block the amendment removes. The loopback judgment is also absent from the five-block copy list in §`apps/registry`.
findings.fix: "The predicate is `IpAddr::is_loopback()`, the one `probe()` uses today at `catalog.rs:248`, applied here to the listener's `local_addr()`" — and either add it to the copy list or mark it as the registry's own.

findings.location: §The serving face step 1 ("after the first `/`, exactly one non-empty `.`-free component, no embedded `/`") + §Catalog document and its spec ("a `source_key` failing `spells_lookup_key` (A16) or the tightened key grammar of §The serving face step 1") + §Budgets ("any `slug` failing §The serving face step 1's validator by name")
findings.problem: The new validator's dot ban makes the registry's admitted lookup-key vocabulary narrower than every shipped spelling rule for the same keys: Source::spells_lookup_key (crates/discovery/src/game.rs:84-89) admits any non-empty external id after a closed-set token, Source::lookup_key (game.rs:66-68) — the single composer, Source::ALL including Source::Local — imposes nothing, and the shipped store validates a slug as exactly "len ≤ MAX_DISCOVERY_SLUG_OCTETS + spells_lookup_key" (apps/discovery-cli/src/matches.rs:222-234). So `local/Steam.SE` is a legal slug the shipped client stores and sends as `slug=`, and this revision refuses it at four seams at once: candidate query (404), admin upsert (refused by name — closing ADR-026's own local/<dir> curation path: "a `local/<dir>` install has a lookup key", "giving `local/`-source installs a curation path no public root can own"), corpus load (a curated corpus can never carry such a key), and cache load (one dotted slug refuses the whole cache document). The rule's stated rationale ("the grammar that keeps a `..` or a separator from ever asking the filesystem for a path") is disclaimed by the same paragraph ("Lookup keys are opaque in-memory strings, never joined onto paths"), and its named precedent is_slug_name governs game_id, already bound by A4. Nothing shipped breaks today (crates/discovery/src/steam_common.rs:249 composes only steam/<appid>), so this is a vocabulary narrowing T-005…T-007 would encode into the wire contract the ADR says stands untouched.
findings.fix: In §The serving face step 1 replace "exactly one non-empty `.`-free component, no embedded `/`" with "exactly one non-empty component with no embedded `/`" and move the dot ban to where its precedent lives — one clause naming is_slug_name/A4 as the game_id-only rule; carry the same substitution into the §Catalog document refusal list and the §Budgets cache-load clause, and re-word #3 and #4 so a dotted `local/…` key is an admitted spelling rather than a 404/refusal. If the ban is wanted, keep it deliberately: say so there, name it as a narrowing of 026's `local/<dir>` use case, and name which task refuses dotted local keys loudly — replacing the path-safety rationale the paragraph already disclaims.

findings.location: §Catalog document and its spec — "`crates/core/tests/conformance.rs`: guard the fixture-tree loops — `every_valid_fixture_…`, both `every_invalid_fixture_…` message tests, and `fixture_file_names_…` (which keeps governing the `.json` fixtures: lowercase dash-separated names, case-unique) — behind the core-TOML check"
findings.problem: The sentence says both that fixture_file_names_… is moved behind the core-TOML check (so it does not run for catalog) and that it "keeps governing the `.json` fixtures"; the instruction is undecidable as written. The property at stake is a platform one: fixture_file_names_are_lowercase_ascii_dash_separated_and_case_unique (crates/core/tests/conformance.rs:336-376) walks format_dirs() — the same walk that picks catalog/v1 up automatically — and its doc-comment names what it buys: names "case-unique within a fixture directory, which is what keeps the same corpus green on a contributor's case-insensitive Windows filesystem as on the Linux CI runner". That is the only coverage behind the Windows `Yes` row's corpus claim and Test #19's "case-unique fixture names". Mechanically related: is_fixture_name takes a bare file name (crates/core/tests/common/mod.rs:421-435), so "accepts `.json` for that directory only" already requires the predicate to learn the directory, and whether this test is guarded decides whether that widening is ever exercised.
findings.fix: Drop `fixture_file_names_…` from the guarded list instead of guarding it with a parenthetical that reverses the guard, and state the reason in the common/mod.rs bullet: "`is_fixture_name` takes the format name (or a per-directory suffix set) so the unguarded `fixture_file_names_…` walk keeps its lowercase/`-`-separated and case-uniqueness rule over `catalog/v1`'s `.json` corpus — the Windows case-insensitive-filesystem claim's only coverage." Text replacement only; no new mechanism.

findings.location: §Compatibility matrix — "| Linux & other Unix | Yes |" plus the new footer "the three `Yes` rows (Linux & other-Unix CI, macOS, Windows) are the rows the tasks owe behavior to", against "| Other / exotic Unix (BSD et al.) | No | Not a v1 target … nothing exercises or promises it."
findings.problem: The r1 fix decided the fourth row but landed on a label that overlaps the first: "other Unix" is simultaneously a Yes the tasks owe behavior to and "not a v1 target … nothing promises it". A T-005…T-008 author cannot tell whether a BSD build is owed behavior or explicitly refused — the same failure mode as an undecided row under two names.
findings.fix: Rename the first row's label to the platform it actually promises — "Linux" (its Notes already say "Primary CI target") — and the footer's parenthetical to "(Linux CI, macOS, Windows)"; if the design means to promise the generic-Unix data-dir branch beyond BSD, give it its own row with its own status instead of hiding it inside row 1's "other Unix". Labels only; #19 already names the three supported platforms and needs no change.

findings.location: §Catalog document and its spec — "`crates/discovery/tests/boundary_tests.rs`: … so re-scope the sweep to `data/manifests` + `data/profiles`, with its doc-comment and `checked > 0` guard re-pinned"
findings.problem: The amendment removes coverage nobody asked it to remove. Shipped shape (crates/discovery/tests/boundary_tests.rs:110-156): the sweep reads every file under `data/` and every `schemas/<format>/<major>/fixtures/valid/`, and its doc-comment pins "no source key or friendly name reaches a manifest, a profile, or a path" against exactly those trees. 026-S1 requires only that `data/catalog/` and `schemas/catalog/v1/` be exempt; re-scoping to the two data/ directories also drops `schemas/manifests/v1/` and `schemas/profile/v{1,2}/` valid fixtures — the trees the pinned rule names — from the gate, permanently.
findings.fix: Replace the re-scope with a carve-out that moves coverage only where 026-S1 forces it: "keep both current roots; skip files under `data/catalog/` and `schemas/catalog/`; amend the doc-comment to name `catalog` as the one tree where a lookup key is legal content". The `checked > 0` guard then needs no re-pinning (data/manifests/ and data/profiles/ are counted either way).

findings.location: §`apps/registry` CLI surface ("relocated in tests through the same env seam as #13") + Test #13 ("this seam is how caching tests relocate the local-entries document (no dedicated CLI knob)")
findings.problem: Dropping `--local-entries <path>` leaves the copied `<data>` rule's env inputs as the only relocation lever, and the design names the seam (the in-process StoreLayout/data_dir env closure, apps/discovery-cli/src/matches.rs:46-103) without naming the variables, while #17's caching end-to-end runs `registry serve --upstream` as a subprocess that writes both catalog-v1.json and cache-v1.json.
findings.fix: One clause in #13: "for the subprocess cases (#17), set `XDG_DATA_HOME` (Unix) / `APPDATA` (Windows) in the child environment; there is no path knob" — so the task author doesn't reintroduce a flag to compensate.

findings.location: Test strategy #3 — "the cap and the key validator apply to **decoded** `slug` and decoded `DELETE` path segment"
findings.problem: The key validator requires `<source-token>/<component>`, so applied literally to a DELETE path segment it would 404 every valid `game_id`; §Admin face correctly pins the DELETE segment to the A4 slug grammar, and the security property (dot/separator rejection via `is_slug_name`, which excludes `.` and `/`) survives, but the test line as written pins the wrong predicate pair.
findings.fix: In #3, pin `slug` against the key validator plus `025-B1`'s cap, and the DELETE segment against the A4 grammar.

findings.location: Chosen design → `http.rs` module line — "a `Transfer-Encoding`, missing or non-decimal length, or an over-cap body is refused before any mutation"
findings.problem: Read literally, "missing length is refused" contradicts the A1-pinned shipped client, whose GETs carry no `Content-Length`; the hand-written reader needs the zero-body case named (`Transfer-Encoding` ⇒ refusal; `Content-Length` present ⇒ read exactly that many octets within cap; absent ⇒ zero-length body) so the request-side framing rule has exactly one reading at the smuggling seam.
findings.fix: Add the zero-`Content-Length`-means-zero-body clause so the framing refusal targets body claims only.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets — "`MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` (1,048,576), `fs::metadata`-gated before the read of the `--corpus` or local-entries file"
findings.problem: The cache got a write-time dual-cap invariant, but the corpus cap is checked only at read, so the authenticated admin face can grow the corpus past 1 MiB and the next start refuses to load it — a token-holder-only self-DoS (the token-holder's integrity damage is the already-accepted 026-R1 risk), asymmetric with the cache's stated posture.
findings.fix: One clause: an upsert whose record would push the document over `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` is refused by name at write, mirroring "provably inside both caps after every mutation".

findings.location: Chosen design → The admin face and auth, "Concurrency (open Q10)" ("mutations take the write lock, mutate the model, and perform the atomic tmp-and-rename under a separate persist-only lock, so serving reads never wait on filesystem IO")
findings.problem: re-raised: the r0 stall is only removed if the model write lock is released before the persist, and the sentence does not say so — std::sync::RwLock blocks new shared readers while a writer holds it, so a mutation that keeps the write lock across the tmp-write/rename reproduces the r0 stall with a second lock added. Three further consequences of the same under-specification: (a) if the persist serializes a snapshot taken at mutation time rather than the model's current state under the persist lock, two mutations can complete their persists out of order and the file can end at an older revision than one already served; (b) the paragraph names Arc<RwLock<Cache>> only in passing, yet in caching mode the ordinary request path is a model mutation plus a write-through rewrite of up to 026-B2 octets, so whether that rewrite runs under the Cache write lock, and whether "a separate persist-only lock" is one lock shared with the corpus persist or one per document, decides whether a cold lookup's disk IO stalls warm candidate reads or an admin POST's persist stalls every cache write; (c) §The serving face step 2 now puts the slug→candidates postings in corpus.rs and nothing says whether a mutation updates that game's postings in place or rebuilds the index under the write lock.
findings.fix: One sentence fixing the protocol: take the model write lock, mutate the model and update that game's postings at their sorted position (no rebuild), release it, then under a per-document persist lock serialize the model's current state and rename; and state that the caching-mode cache write-through follows the same order with its own persist lock, so "serving reads never wait on filesystem IO" holds on the hot path, not only for admin mutations.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets (request-budgets paragraph), with §apps/registry serve.rs and the Risks row "Low-and-slow / one-inbound-per-outbound exposure on a routable bind" ("MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS (over-cap closed at accept, one thread per admitted connection)")
findings.problem: re-raised: this is the only budget in the constants.rs list with no value — the two request budgets carry 65,536, the corpus and cache carry 1,048,576, the TTL carries 3,600. Under thread-per-connection with no runtime or pool, that number is the peak-thread and peak-stack-reservation bound for the flagship 026-C5 routable public root, so the growth bound r0 asked for is nominal: Test-strategy #11 cannot pin an assertion to a value, T-005 will choose one arbitrarily, and an operator sizing a public root has no capacity expectation.
findings.fix: Give the constant a default in the same parenthetical (a stated value, optionally overridable by --max-connections) and name that default in #11's assertion.

findings.location: Caching mode → "Upstream reachability" ("probed at most once per TTL, fired lazily by the first lookup or health read after expiry on that request's own thread — there is no timer thread … A query pays no health round trip beyond that one TTL-gated probe")
findings.problem: new: naming the lazy driver closes r0's question but relies on an amortization bound nothing enforces — with one thread per connection, several threads can pass the expiry test before the verdict stamp is written, so "at most once per TTL" is a claim about intent, not a property, and each extra probe costs the mirrored 2 s connect / 5 s read on a serving thread. Compounding it, --refresh-interval "overrides 026-B3" with no stated floor, so a small operator-set TTL degrades the bound toward a synchronous upstream probe per request on both /v1/candidates and /v1/health — the per-request synchronous IO this revision exists to avoid.
findings.fix: One clause making the probe single-flight (the thread that compare-and-sets the last_upstream_fetch stamp under the Cache write lock is the only one that probes for that TTL; the rest serve the previous verdict) and one clause stating the floor for --refresh-interval (at least the upstream read timeout).

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets ("after a write the registry evicts the oldest entry by insertion sequence (ties by fetched_at, …)")
findings.problem: new: the switch from fetched_at order to insertion order fixes the clock-jump hazard, but the document never says whether a warm hit (Caching mode step 2, "Cached entry within TTL answers as-is") moves the entry to the newest sequence. If it does not, eviction is FIFO, and with the design's own accepted working set (≈16 fat / ≈90 realistic entries, or a few thousand thin ones under 026-B1) a burst of cold slugs evicts the hot ones and the next query pays another serial upstream round trip.
findings.fix: One clause naming the policy — either "a warm hit re-stamps the entry's insertion sequence (LRU)" or "eviction is FIFO by insertion sequence; a hot slug may be evicted by cold churn" — so T-007's eviction test pins the right behavior.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets ("026-B2 is re-checked at load" read against "MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS (1,048,576), fs::metadata-gated before the read of the --corpus or local-entries file")
findings.problem: new: the revision applies the pre-allocation gate to the two catalog documents but not to the third load path, the cache file: as written an oversized cache-v1.json is read and parsed before 026-B2 refuses it. Both precedents the design invokes gate before allocating (apps/discovery-cli/src/matches.rs:194; crates/core/src/toml.rs:51-58, "refused without being allocated"), and the ADR's 026-B2 itself says "refused by name like the match store's".
findings.fix: Extend that parenthetical to "… or local-entries file, and the cache read is gated at 026-B2 the same way", with the refusal noted in Test-strategy #5.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets ("MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS (65,536, sized to one 026-C3 record inside the document cap)")
findings.problem: new: the "sized to" justification does not close — 026-C3 bounds each source_key by 025-B1 and name by 013-B4 but nothing bounds the number of source_keys on one record (no shipped or proposed count cap exists), so a record with a few hundred keys is legal at load under the 1 MiB document cap while being refuseable as a POST body, leaving a hand-edited local-entries record the server loaded but its own admin face can never upsert.
findings.fix: Bound source_keys per record with a constants.rs count cap chosen so one record fits inside MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS, refused by name in the corpus.rs refusal list and Test-strategy #1; or re-word the parenthetical so the body cap is stated as the per-record cap that load also enforces.

findings.location: §Budgets — "evicts the oldest entry by insertion sequence (ties by fetched_at, so a backwards clock jump cannot make fresh data the eviction target)" + "The in-memory cache holds each entry's serialized octet count with a running total … O(1) plus evictions, never a whole-document re-serialization"
findings.problem: The r1 rewrite changed the eviction key 026-B1 names (ADR-026: "over the cap the oldest fetched_at is evicted"), demoting fetched_at to a tie-break. Test strategy #4 keeps the cache document "sorted by slug byte order", so after any restart insertion sequence IS slug order and eviction silently becomes alphabetical — entries die because their slug sorts low, not because they are old, and #5 as written pins that wrong key for T-007. The machinery also buys nothing: the same section says the file is rewritten write-through after each lookup that adds an entry, so every write already serializes the whole ≤1 MiB document; the per-entry octet totals, the running total and the insertion counter (plus the tie-break existing only to defuse clock jumps) are three bookkeeping parts traced to no stated Goal, and "provably inside both caps" ends up resting on a sum of entry lengths, which is not the document's length.
findings.fix: Replace the insertion-sequence clause with 026-B1's oldest-fetched_at eviction plus a single write-time serialize whose buffer length is the byte check (exact, no per-entry totals); delete the running total, the per-entry octet count and the insertion sequence, keeping the existing load bound and backwards-jump guard for clock jumps; change #5 to pin eviction by fetched_at.

findings.location: §The serving face step 1 — "the registry's one key validator tightens it: after the first `/`, exactly one non-empty `.`-free component, no embedded `/` — the grammar that keeps a `..` or a separator from ever asking the filesystem for a path" with "Lookup keys are opaque in-memory strings, never joined onto paths"
findings.problem: A second, registry-private spelling rule for keys the repo validates in exactly one place: the shipped validator is Source::spells_lookup_key plus len ≤ MAX_DISCOVERY_SLUG_OCTETS with no character or dot rule (apps/discovery-cli/src/matches.rs:222-234, 282-283; crates/discovery/src/game.rs:84-89 admits any non-empty external id after a closed-set token), so a dotted key such as `local/Steam.SE` is legal in the user's own store and refused by this fourth grammar site at three seams (candidate query, admin upsert via §Catalog document and its spec, cache load via §Budgets). Its sole stated purpose is path safety, which the very next sentence disclaims, and its cited precedent is_slug_name governs game_id, already bound by A4 — an added rule with no consumer and a contract-divergence cost.
findings.fix: Keep the shipped pair (spells_lookup_key + 025-B1) as the registry's whole key rule; if the path-safety defense is wanted, keep only its real scope in one clause (a component equal to `.` or `..`, or any further `/` after the first, is the 404) and drop the flat `.`-ban from step 1, from the corpus-load refusal list, and from #3/#4's dot-bearing case.

findings.location: §Budgets — "One saturated entry is MAX_RESPONSE_OCTETS (≈64 KiB), so 026-B2 alone caps the working set at ≈16 fat entries (≈90 at realistic ~40-octet candidates) — accepted; #5 and cached_slugs read expect that, not 5,000."
findings.problem: The realistic band is wrong by an order of magnitude and no per-entry figure is shown. A1 pins MAX_RESPONSE_OCTETS = 65_536 (catalog.rs:23), so 16 entries is the at-the-cap worst case only; a realistic entry (slug + {game_id,name} + fetched_at + JSON framing) is on the order of 10^2 octets, so ~10^3–10^4 entries fit inside 1 MiB and 026-B1's 5,000 is the cap that binds for ordinary answers — which is what #5 states. The sentence is load-bearing twice: it justifies accepting the ≈16-entry working set and it tells the T-007 test author what cached_slugs should reach, contradicting #5's `count ≤ 5_000` in the same list.
findings.fix: State the assumed per-entry octet figure and name which cap binds in which band (byte cap near MAX_CANDIDATES, 026-B1 for ordinary answers), and delete the "#5 and cached_slugs read expect that, not 5,000" instruction.

findings.location: §Budgets — "MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS (over-cap closed at accept, one thread per admitted connection)" (also §serve.rs, §Risks, #11)
findings.problem: The only one of the five new constants carried without a value, while #11 pins behavior against it ("over-MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS is closed at accept"). It is also the sole bound on live thread count and, in caching mode, on simultaneous upstream hops each of which may hold the mirrored 2 s/5 s timeouts, a product the design never states. §Budgets' stated job is that budgets close against each other, and the task author must invent the number the proposal exists to decide.
findings.fix: Give the value in the same sentence (e.g. 64) and cite it in #11 by value, as the other four constants now are.

findings.location: §Caching mode — "probed at most once per TTL, fired lazily by the first lookup or health read after expiry on that request's own thread" vs §The serving face — "Answering it reads the last-known upstream verdict … it does not perform a live upstream probe per call"
findings.problem: The sentence that supplied the missing refresh trigger also made a health read a probe trigger, which is precisely what the health section promises the 026-C2 route never does; the two sections now contradict each other about the same route's behavior.
findings.fix: Drop "or health read" so only lookups drive the TTL-gated probe and a health read reports the last-known verdict; alternatively move the health trigger into the health paragraph, qualified as at most one probe per TTL.

findings.location: §Catalog document and its spec — "guard the fixture-tree loops — every_valid_fixture_…, both every_invalid_fixture_… message tests, and fixture_file_names_… (which keeps governing the .json fixtures: lowercase dash-separated names, case-unique) — behind the core-TOML check so catalog fixtures are not parsed as TOML"
findings.problem: The bullet both guards the fixture-name test for the catalog format and says that test keeps governing catalog's .json fixtures — opposite instructions. In the shipped harness, fixture_file_names_are_lowercase_ascii_dash_separated_and_case_unique walks format_dirs() and asserts is_fixture_name(name) per file, so guarded means catalog's fixture names go uncontrolled; and is_fixture_name (crates/core/tests/common/mod.rs:421) hard-codes the .toml suffix and takes no format argument, so leaving it unguarded without the new argument fails the walk.
findings.fix: One sentence per loop: the parse and rejection loops are guarded for the catalog format, while fixture_file_names_… is not skipped and instead calls the directory-aware is_fixture_name(dir, name) — which is what actually keeps the name and case-uniqueness rule on the .json fixtures.

findings.location: §CLI surface — "--refresh-interval overrides 026-B3 (default REGISTRY_UPSTREAM_TTL_SECONDS = 3_600)"
findings.problem: The pass retired the unconsumed --local-entries knob but left this one with no consumer anywhere in the Test strategy: #6 pins fresh/stale/cold against an injected fake, #12 pins health, #17 chains a caching instance, and none shortens the TTL.
