The knob itself must stay (026-B3 mandates "overridable by --refresh-interval"), and the same interval now also re-times the TTL-gated upstream probe, which nothing observes.
findings.fix: Add one clause to #6: start a caching instance with --refresh-interval 0 (or 1 s) and pin that a previously fresh entry is stale on the next query and triggers the refresh; note there that the override also re-times the health probe.

findings.location: §Concurrency (open Q10) — "mutations take the write lock, mutate the model, and perform the atomic tmp-and-rename under a separate persist-only lock, so serving reads never wait on filesystem IO"
findings.problem: r1 added a third lock domain for a benefit no Goal or ADR unit states (the cache is ≤1 MiB and the corpus is a local file; no Goal prices a reader waiting on one local write), and the split decouples persist order from model order: two accepted mutations can reach the tmp-and-rename in the opposite order, leaving the file at the older revision while memory holds the newer, so after a restart an accepted mutation is gone. Nothing in #10 or #11 pins persist order, so either outcome ships with the tests green.
findings.fix: Do the tmp-and-rename while holding the model write lock (the r0 wording: one lock, ordered) and delete the persist-only lock; if read latency ever earns its keep, name it as a refinement beside the copy lift in §Deferred.

findings.location: §The admin face and auth — "Enablement is judged from the address actually bound — the shipped probe() predicate local_addr().ip().is_loopback(), not a literal-spelling comparison"
findings.problem: The quoted expression is not the shipped one: probe() (apps/discovery-cli/src/catalog.rs:234-248) applies is_loopback() to each resolved address, and local_addr appears nowhere in that function, so a T-006 author going to the named precedent will not find it.
findings.fix: Reword to "the same std::net::IpAddr::is_loopback test probe() applies to each resolved address, applied here to the serving listener's local_addr()".

findings.location: §apps/registry — one crate, two modes — "and on discovery for Source and spells_lookup_key"
findings.problem: The new dependency edge is taken for a two-line token predicate and pulls the whole engine crate into the serving binary, including its Windows-only winreg dependency (crates/discovery/Cargo.toml:38-39) that the registry never uses; the Compatibility matrix's Windows | Yes row is silent about it. Reusing the authoritative predicate is right, so this is record-keeping.
findings.fix: Either state in that sentence that the dep is for the predicate alone and the transitive Windows cost is accepted, or name the alternative once beside the existing lift in §Deferred (give Source/spells_lookup_key the same shared home as the copied blocks so apps/registry depends on bindforge-core only).

reply.summary: All three r1c1 reports consumed by changing the design, not appending to it: the concurrency passage reverts to a single model write lock holding the tmp-and-rename and the persist-only lock plus its "reads never wait on IO" promise are deleted (correctness major / complexity major); the cache's insertion-sequence key, per-entry octet totals and running total are deleted in favour of `026-B1`'s own oldest-`fetched_at` eviction and an exact write-buffer byte test, and the ≈16-fat-entry acceptance line is gone (complexity major, correctness regression); the registry-private `.`-ban key grammar is deleted so the shipped `spells_lookup_key` + `025-B1` pair is the whole rule with path safety stated only at its own scope (correctness/compatibility/complexity majors), carrying into the corpus refusal list, the cache-load clause and #3/#4; the fixture-name test is un-guarded behind a directory-aware `is_fixture_name`, and the `boundary_tests` sweep keeps both roots and skips only `data/catalog/` + `schemas/catalog/` instead of the re-scope (compatibility/complexity minors, plus the Options nit and the Risks mitigation); `or health read` is dropped from the probe trigger so health never fires it (correctness/complexity minors); `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` is re-sized to 16,777,216 with its arithmetic in `spec.md`, `MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS` becomes the document cap instead of an unsatisfiable sizing claim, and `MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS` gets 64 with its over-cap answer and per-connection thread story; matrix row 1 is relabelled `Linux` with the footer corrected; and #1 gains the within-record repeated `source_key` refusal, #5 pins `fetched_at` eviction, #6 pins `--refresh-interval`, #11 pins file-equals-model after concurrent mutations, #13 names the child-env seam, with the `probe()` attribution, `discovery`/`winreg` note and Revision log updated in place. Net line count is positive (+29) because the seats asked for constant values, refusal-list entries and six new pinned test assertions that the deleted machinery (persist lock, eviction bookkeeping, private grammar, sweep re-scope) did not occupy in the same places.
reply.commitMessage: docs: revise 026 registry proposal for r1c1 design-review findings

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets / The admin face and auth — "`MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS` (= `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS`, so any record a loadable corpus could legally hold also fits an upsert and no per-record `source_keys` bound is needed)" and, in §Catalog document and its spec, the cap placed only in the loader's list: "a document over `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` (§Budgets)"
findings.problem: The corpus document cap has no write-time rule anywhere in the design, while the cache cap now has one ("after a write the registry serializes the cache … until the buffer is ≤ `026-B2` octets"). An accepted `POST /v1/admin/games` can therefore persist a corpus whose serialized length passes 16,777,216, and the next start refuses the whole corpus by name — every accepted mutation on it is lost, which falsifies the sentence this revision just added to §Concurrency ("a restart cannot lose an accepted mutation (#11)"). Both reachable paths are newly opened by this revision: (a) the body cap was raised from 65,536 to the document cap, so a single legal upsert (026-C3 bounds each source_key by 025-B1 and the design now names no per-record bound) can push an empty corpus past the cap in one accepted request; (b) the document cap was raised to the ADR's "tens of thousands of games" scale, so a root corpus living at the cap is now a supported configuration (under r1's 1 MiB it was already an error), making ordinary curation across the line the normal operator path. 026-C4 requires "every accepted mutation bumps `revision` and persists atomically", yet the design never states what POST answers when the resulting document would be unloadable: #10 pins only "upsert validates + bumps `revision` + atomic rename" and #11's over-cap refusal is a per-request body bound, not a resulting-document bound. T-006 implements this with no pinned answer.
findings.fix: Replace "validated against `026-C3` and refused by name; bumps `revision`; persists atomically through the tmp-and-rename discipline" with "validated against `026-C3` and refused by name; the write is then completed by serializing the whole document and refusing, by name, `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` as a `422` that leaves `revision`, the model and the file untouched; only then does `revision` bump and the tmp-and-rename run (the loader's over-cap refusal stays as the same rule's read side)", add that refusal to `schemas/catalog/v1/spec.md`'s roster next to the record-level ones, and pin in #10: "an upsert whose serialized corpus would pass `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` is the named `422`, `revision` unchanged, no tmp written".

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets — "after a write the registry serializes the cache once and drops the oldest-`fetched_at` entries … until the buffer is ≤ `026-B2` octets and the entry count ≤ `026-B1`, then renames that buffer into place, so the octet test is the document's exact length and not a sum of per-entry totals"
findings.problem: The two halves pull apart: measuring "the document's exact length" after each drop requires a re-serialization per eviction, while subtracting each dropped entry's length from one buffer is exactly the "sum of per-entry totals" the clause disclaims.
findings.fix: Replace "serializes the cache once" with "serializes the cache, and re-serializes after each dropped entry (at most one extra pass per eviction)", leaving the rest of the sentence.

findings.location: Chosen design → The admin face and auth, Concurrency — "a persist-only lock to cut that latency joins §Deferred's lift if it ever earns its keep"
findings.problem: §Deferred's lift entry is "Lifting the five copied invariant blocks … into a shared crate" and carries no persist lock; a latency mechanism is deferred to a list that does not contain it, and that lift is a code-sharing refactor rather than a latency item.
findings.fix: Add "and, if #11's N-upsert latency ever matters, the persist-only lock §Concurrency deletes" to that §Deferred bullet, or drop the pointer and state the "reader may wait on one local write" latency as accepted.

findings.location: Chosen design → Catalog document and its spec, harness list — "`fixture_file_names_are_lowercase_ascii_dash_separated_and_case_unique` is **not** guarded … which is the only coverage behind the Windows `Yes` row's case-insensitive-filesystem claim (#19)"
findings.problem: The Compatibility matrix's Windows row makes no case-insensitivity claim in either its r1 or r2 form ("`<data>` = `%APPDATA%` … owner-only modes are a documented no-op … cache and local-entries paths …"); the case-collision claim is #19's ("**Windows** and **macOS** behavior is proven by the env-closure seam (#13) and case-unique fixture names"), so the rationale cites a matrix claim that is not there.
findings.fix: Say "the only coverage behind #19's case-unique-fixture-name claim for a case-insensitive filesystem", or add the case-collision note to the Windows row so the pointer lands.

findings.location: §The serving face step 1 — "Path safety is the only extra refusal, at its own scope: after the first `/`, one non-empty component with no further `/` or `\`, none equal to `.` or `..`, and no control byte, space, or invalid-UTF-8 sequence" (carried into §Catalog document and its spec, §Budgets' cache-load clause, and #1/#3/#4)
findings.problem: re-raised (narrowed from r1's major; the dot case is closed). The space ban is not a path-safety refusal, and the same paragraph's parenthetical says lookup keys are "opaque in-memory strings, never joined onto paths" — yet the sentence above it claims "that shipped pair is the registry's whole key rule". Shipped evidence: Source::spells_lookup_key (crates/discovery/src/game.rs:84-89) admits any non-empty external id after a closed-set token; Source::lookup_key (game.rs:66-68), the single composer, imposes nothing further; the shipped store's only slug checks are the 025-B1 cap plus spells_lookup_key (apps/discovery-cli/src/matches.rs:222-234); and the shipped client puts such a key on the wire, escaping a space as %20 (catalog.rs:174-185, A19). So a space-bearing 025-C1 key — the local/<dir> external id, whose only stated derivation law is "the kebab'd install directory name" with no grammar — is refused at all four seams this rule governs: candidate query (404), admin upsert (refused by name), corpus load, and cache load (one such slug refuses the whole cache document). The document is also internally split: #3 admits the non-kebab'd `local/Steam.SE` (lenient reading of the derivation) while this clause refuses a space (strict reading), so T-005 cannot tell which vocabulary it is pinning. Blast radius is much smaller than r1's dot case — no shipped emitter produces a space today — hence minor rather than major.
findings.fix: Delete `space` from the banned set, leaving "no control byte or invalid-UTF-8 sequence", so the extra refusals are exactly the named path-safety and line-integrity classes; nothing else changes because every dependent seam already references this one clause. If a space ban is wanted on some other ground, keep it but state that ground here and name it as a narrowing of the 025-C1/026-C3 key vocabulary that no shipped spelling rule shares.

findings.location: §Budgets — "`MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS` (= `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS`, so any record a loadable corpus could legally hold also fits an upsert and no per-record `source_keys` bound is needed)" with "`MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` (16,777,216 — ≈120,000 records …), `fs::metadata`-gated before the read"
findings.problem: This round's new equivalence closes only one direction: the corpus's 16 MiB cap exists at load only (§Catalog document's refusal list, §Budgets' metadata gate, #1), while §The admin face lets accepted mutations grow that same document with no counterpart check — so a root can be driven past the size its own loader refuses and then not restart until the operator hand-edits the JSON. The cap is sized at exactly the ADR's projected scale ("tens of thousands of games, each with several store keys"), so growth across it is foreseeable, not exotic; this is the same reasoning §Options used to reject refuse-the-file-alone for the cache ("it does not stop a legal-but-large corpus … from exceeding 1 MiB between writes"), yet the corpus/cache asymmetry is recorded nowhere and #10/#11 pin revision and persist order but never size. The bound declined (a per-record `source_keys` count) is precisely what the enlarged body cap is claimed to make unnecessary.
findings.fix: Reuse the mechanism §Budgets just defined instead of adding one: "the corpus persist applies the same write-buffer check — a mutation whose serialized document exceeds `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` is refused by name, no rename" (the persist is already under the one write lock per §Concurrency); add that refusal to §Catalog document's list and one case to #11. If the asymmetry is instead deliberate, say so in one clause and restore the r1 per-record `source_keys` bound with the 64 KiB body cap so the loadable-corpus claim is not load-only.

findings.location: §`apps/registry` modules — "`serve.rs` — accept loop (one thread per admitted connection, covering that connection's whole request loop, up to `MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS`, over-cap closed at accept…)" plus §Budgets' "one thread per admitted connection for that connection's whole life, so ≤64 live threads and ≤64 in-flight upstream hops"
findings.problem: r1 said one thread per connection; r2 adds a per-connection request loop — a mechanism with no consumer, since the only client this face must satisfy sends `Connection: close` with one request per connection (apps/discovery-cli/src/catalog.rs:438, A19) and §http.rs never states whether the connection is closed after the answer. The phrase also undercuts the bound it was added to state: with a keep-alive loop an idle client holds one of the 64 admitted slots for the connection's whole life (bounded only by the read timeout), which is exactly when the "≤64 in-flight upstream hops" claim matters.
findings.fix: Replace the phrase with "one request-response per admitted connection, then close, echoing the shipped client's `Connection: close`" and add that close to §http.rs; if keep-alive is intended, name it as such in the same sentence together with the idle-slot timeout that bounds it.

findings.location: §Test strategy #6 — "with the fresh/stale pair run under `--refresh-interval 1s`" (with §CLI surface's "`--refresh-interval` overrides `026-B3` (default `REGISTRY_UPSTREAM_TTL_SECONDS = 3_600`)")
findings.problem: The flag's value spelling is never defined and the case added this round depends on it: the budget is a count of seconds, so a `u64`-seconds parser rejects `1s` and the new #6 case fails on a parse error rather than on the policy it means to pin.
findings.fix: State the unit once at the knob ("`--refresh-interval <seconds>`") and write the case as `--refresh-interval 1`.

findings.location: §The serving face step 1 — "Path safety is the only extra refusal, at its own scope: after the first `/`, one non-empty component with no further `/` or `\`, none equal to `.` or `..`, and no control byte, space, or invalid-UTF-8 sequence"
findings.problem: The `space` item is the only entry in the list that is not path safety: it cannot traverse or split a path, and it cannot break the one-line refusal discipline the control-byte ban already protects, while the same sentence keeps keys as "opaque in-memory strings, never joined onto paths". It is also the one clause that can still 404 a key the shipped pair admits — `spells_lookup_key` (crates/discovery/src/game.rs:84-89) and `Source::lookup_key` (game.rs:66-68) impose nothing on the external id, the shipped store checks only that pair plus `025-B1` (apps/discovery-cli/src/matches.rs:229,282), and the client sends any such key escaping a space as `%20` — with `local/<dir>`, the ADR's own example of what the admin face exists to curate, the natural home of a space-bearing id. Nothing shipped emits one today, hence nit.
findings.fix: Drop "space" from the refusal list, or keep it and name in one clause the `local/` key-derivation law it enforces.

reply.summary: Correctness major + complexity major (same seam, one canonical rule): `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` is now a write-time invariant too — §The admin face's `POST /v1/admin/games` serializes the upserted model whole and answers the named `422` (A21) with model, `revision`, file and tmp untouched before any rename, §Budgets states the cap is enforced at both ends of a document's life and cites #10, §Catalog document's refusal list names the load as the read side of that same rule, and `spec.md`'s roster gains the write-side refusal; no accepted mutation can now persist a corpus its own loader refuses. Complexity minor (per-connection request loop): the phrase is deleted from `serve.rs`, `http.rs` now answers one request per connection and closes (new A23 pins the shipped client's `Connection: close`), and §Budgets' thread story follows it, so no idle client holds one of the 64 slots. Correctness nit (eviction measurement): §Budgets says the cache is re-serialized after each dropped entry, so "the document's exact length" is no longer contradicted by a single serialize. Correctness nit (§Deferred pointer): the persist-only-lock pointer is deleted and the one-local-write wait is stated as accepted, so §Deferred's lift is no longer pointed at by a mechanism it does not contain. Correctness nit (Windows row citation): the fixture-name-test rationale now cites #19's case-unique-name claim, not a matrix claim that does not exist. Complexity nit (`1s`): the knob is `--refresh-interval <seconds>`, a bare unsigned count, and #6 runs it as `--refresh-interval 1`. Complexity nit (space refusal): "space" is deleted from the path-safety list in §The serving face step 1. Revision log maintained in place — the §Budgets, §Concurrency, §Serving face step 1, §Catalog document and health entries are superseded where they stand, no stacked corrections. Net +3 lines (645→648) because the two majors required a new binding refusal, its test pin and a register row; offset by deleting the persist-only-lock clause, the keep-alive loop, the space refusal, the duplicated bearer-over-plaintext and `winreg`-lift sentences, the redundant `Defaults` and rollout-step-7 copies, and a restated `026-S1` sweep clause.
reply.commitMessage: docs: enforce the catalog document cap on admin writes in the registry proposal

findings.location: Chosen design → The serving face step 1 / Caching mode (upstream client) — "Miss with reachable upstream fetches `GET <upstream>/v1/candidates?slug=`, validates the answer, and caches it", read against §`apps/registry`'s closed copy list ("five invariants are copied … the response reader (#7), the endpoint gate (#14, #15), the `game_id_is_valid` predicate (#8), the `<data>` rule (#13), and the tmp-and-rename persist (#10, #11)") and the Revision log's r3 line "deletes the space refusal"
findings.problem: [new; introduced by this revision's closure] Widening the admitted key alphabet proves the keys safe against the filesystem ("keys are opaque in-memory strings, never joined onto paths") but never against the wire, and nothing in the design says how the caching registry spells an admitted key in the request line it sends upstream. The shipped `percent_encode`/`candidates_url` request builder (A19) is not among the five copied invariants, and #7 pins only response refusals, so the outbound request target is unspecified. The ADR's own `local/<dir>` case makes this concrete: a directory name with a space is now a legal slug (`local/Steam Big Game`), and fetching `GET /v1/candidates?slug=steam/Steam Big Game` sends a request target with a raw space, which the root's own request reader refuses as a framing fault — the user gets the stale/`503` path for a key their corpus can legally hold. For a `%`-bearing key (also admitted, since `%` is no control byte and no separator) it is worse: forwarding the decoded `steam/foo%2Fbar` raw makes the upstream decode twice, refuse it as a further separator, or answer for a different key, which this registry then caches under its own key — a wrong answer that outlives the request. T-007 must invent this rule, and no §Test strategy item would catch the choice.
findings.fix: Name the shipped `percent_encode`/`candidates_url` discipline (A19) as the sixth copied invariant in §`apps/registry` (and change "five" to "six" in §`apps/registry` and §Deferred, since the lift now carries it too), and replace step 4's "fetches `GET <upstream>/v1/candidates?slug=`, validates the answer, and caches it" with "fetches `GET <upstream>/v1/candidates?slug=`, the request target built from the *decoded* slug through the copied `percent_encode` (A19), so the bytes the upstream decodes are exactly the key this instance asked about, validates the answer, and caches it"; pin it in #7: "a key bearing a space or `%` reaches the upstream only as its encoded spelling".

findings.location: Chosen design → The admin face and auth — "the model with the upsert is then serialized whole, and one over `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` (§Budgets) is the named `422` … leaving model, `revision` and file untouched with no tmp written. Only then does `revision` bump and the tmp-and-rename persist run (A7), under §Concurrency's one lock"
findings.problem: [new; residue of the r1 major's closure] The buffer tested is the pre-bump document, but the bytes renamed into place are the post-bump model (§Concurrency: "a mutation serializes the new model, writes the fixed tmp name, renames it into place"), so the persisted document can be one octet longer than the checked one whenever `revision` grows a digit (9→10, 99→100, …). A corpus serializing to exactly 16,777,216 with `revision` 9 passes the check and persists 16,777,217, and the next start refuses the whole corpus by name — falsifying the two absolutes this revision just wrote: "no accepted mutation can persist a corpus its own loader refuses" (§Budgets) and "a restart cannot lose an accepted mutation (#11)" (§Concurrency).
findings.fix: Order the bump before the check on the candidate model so the buffer tested is the buffer renamed: "the model with the upsert and the next `revision` value is then serialized whole, and one over `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` … is the named `422` … leaving model, `revision` and file untouched with no tmp written; only then is that same buffer written to the fixed tmp, renamed, and the model swapped in"; and in #10, "an upsert whose serialized corpus would pass" → "an upsert whose serialized corpus with its bumped `revision` would pass".

findings.location: §The admin face and auth — "the model with the upsert is then serialized whole, and one over `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` (§Budgets) is the named `422` … leaving model, `revision` and file untouched … Only then does `revision` bump and the tmp-and-rename persist run"
findings.problem: new: the buffer that is checked is not the buffer that is written. `revision` is a serialized field of the document (§Catalog document's `{version, revision, games}`; ADR `026-C3`'s "bumped by every mutation"), so the persisted document is the checked buffer plus the octets the bump adds, and at the boundary (≈16,777,215 octets, or a revision crossing a power of ten) an accepted upsert persists a corpus a few octets over the cap that its own loader then refuses — the exact state §Budgets' new sentence claims cannot happen ("so no accepted mutation can persist a corpus its own loader refuses"). The two clauses also disagree with each other about whether the bump is inside the checked serialization: "the model with the upsert" reads as though it includes it, "Only then does `revision` bump" says it does not. My r1 major is otherwise closed by the right mechanism; this is the ordering residue of the new text.
findings.fix: One clause: serialize the candidate copy with the bump already applied, check that buffer, and have the persist write exactly that buffer, swapping the model (new record + new `revision`) in only after the rename succeeds; then #10 pins the boundary inclusive at the cap with the revision already incremented. No new mechanism — the cache document's §Budgets check has no such hole because `{version, entries}` carries no `revision`, which is precisely why the corpus is the one place the ordering must be stated.

findings.location: §Test strategy #10 — "an upsert whose serialized corpus would pass `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` is that named `422` with model, `revision` and file untouched"
findings.problem: new: "would pass" reads as "satisfies the cap", which inverts the case being pinned. The document's own refusal voice is "over" (#1 "document over `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS`", #5 "load over `026-B2` is refused"), and the r3 Revision-log line repeats the same ambiguous word ("an upsert whose serialized corpus passes it being the named `422`"). A test engineer pinning #10 literally writes the acceptance boundary backwards.
findings.fix: "would exceed `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS`" here and in the Revision-log clause.

findings.location: §Deferred — "Lifting the five copied invariant blocks … into a shared crate so both binaries call one copy, which also gives `Source`/`spells_lookup_key` that shared home"
findings.problem: new: this round's trim deleted the entry's tail ("and retires `apps/registry`'s `discovery` edge with its Windows-only `winreg` transitive"), while §`apps/registry` (unchanged text) still promises that edge is "taken for that predicate and retired by the deferred lift below" — a pointer into text that no longer makes the claim. The claim is true (`crates/discovery/Cargo.toml:39` carries `winreg = { workspace = true }`), so the casualty is the cross-reference, and with it the lift's only stated payoff beyond deduplication.
findings.fix: Restore the retired-transitive clause in the same §Deferred sentence (preferred), or delete "and retired by the deferred lift below" from §`apps/registry`.

reply.summary: Finding 1 (wire spelling of the widened key alphabet): the shipped percent_encode/candidates_url builder is named as the sixth copied invariant in §apps/registry (five→six there and in §Deferred), §Caching mode step 4 now states the upstream request target is built from the decoded slug through that copied builder, and #7 pins a space- or %-bearing slug reaching upstream only percent-encoded. Finding 2 (one-octet revision-digit window): §The admin face and auth now serializes and caps the model with the upsert AND the next revision value — the exact buffer renamed — with the cap check ordered before any tmp write; §Budgets now says the check runs on 'the exact post-revision-bump buffer an admin write renames into place' and #10 adds 'with its bumped revision'. Revision log maintained in place: the §Budgets and §Serving-face-key-alphabet entries' r3 clauses are superseded by current r4 entries in situ, and the §apps/registry dependency entry now records six copied invariants; no stacked corrections. Diff is net +2 lines because both findings resolve by pinning behavior at the outbound hop and the persist ordering, which each add a clause; offsets came from rewrapping and dropping the duplicated lock-scope clause already owned by §Concurrency.
reply.commitMessage: docs: pin upstream request-target encoding and post-bump document-cap check in 026 proposal

findings.location: §Test strategy #10 (**Admin mutations**) — "an upsert whose serialized corpus with its bumped `revision` would pass `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` is that named `422`"
findings.problem: new; in this round's rewritten line. "would pass <a budget>" reads two ways: "exceed it" (the intent, matching §The admin face and auth's "one over `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` … is the named `422`" and §Budgets' "checked against the exact post-`revision`-bump buffer an admin write renames into place") or "satisfy it", which inverts the rule. Every other refusal site in the document uses "over", so this is the only place a test engineer authoring #10 from the item alone could pin the opposite of the contract. Not blocking: the two unambiguous statements elsewhere fix the meaning.
findings.fix: One word: "an upsert whose serialized corpus with its bumped `revision` would exceed `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` is that named `422`".

findings.location: §Deferred / out of scope, lift bullet — "Lifting the six copied invariant blocks (§`apps/registry`) from `apps/discovery-cli` into a shared crate so both binaries call one copy, which also gives `Source`/`spells_lookup_key` that shared home"
findings.problem: The r4 rewrite of this bullet dropped the explicit retirement of `apps/registry`'s `discovery` edge "with its Windows-only `winreg` transitive" that r1 stated here, while §`apps/registry` still promises "retired by the deferred lift below" and the revision-log dependency line still asserts the retirement. The deferral now carries only half of the promise the body points at: its named scope is the six copied client blocks plus a home for `Source`/`spells_lookup_key`, so the OS-specific-dependency consequence must be inferred. No ADR or contract impact; the lift itself still exists and my r1 key-rule finding is fully closed.
findings.fix: Restore the deleted clause into the same bullet: "…, which also gives `Source`/`spells_lookup_key` that shared home and so retires `apps/registry`'s `discovery` edge with its Windows-only `winreg` transitive" — no new scope, one clause.

findings.location: §The serving face step 1 — "Percent-decode `slug` **first**, then apply `025-B1`'s 128-octet cap and `spells_lookup_key` to the *decoded* bytes", read with the r3 space admission ("no control byte or invalid-UTF-8 sequence")
findings.problem: The widened alphabet makes an unspecified part of the decode seam load-bearing. The copied `percent_encode` (A19, verified at apps/discovery-cli/src/catalog.rs:174-185) never emits a bare `+` and escapes `+` as `%2B`, so a percent-decode that also folds `+` to a space (the form-urlencoding habit) turns a shipped-legitimate `local/foo+bar` into `local/foo bar`. Before the space ban was deleted that mistranslation died loudly at the seam; now it yields a legal key, which caching mode then forwards `%20`-encoded (step 4) and caches under, answering a different question than it was asked. The design never authorizes `+`-folding, so this is underspecification introduced by the closure of my own finding, not a contradiction.
findings.fix: In step 1, pin the decode to percent-escapes only: "percent-decode (a literal `+` stays `+`; the only space spelling is `%20`, as the copied `percent_encode` emits)". One parenthetical; #3's `404` list and the outbound hop are unchanged by it.

findings.location: §Budgets → request budgets — "`MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS` (= `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS`, so any record a loadable corpus could legally hold also fits an upsert and no per-record `source_keys` bound is needed)"
findings.problem: The revision moved the inbound request-body bound from the r1 value this seat approved (65,536, "mirroring the client's own header cap") to 16,777,216 for every route, because the constant was re-purposed as the document cap; the §Risks row still cites it as the inbound mitigation ("Low-and-slow / one-inbound-per-outbound exposure on a routable bind … `MAX_REQUEST_HEADER_OCTETS`/`MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS`") while the bound it names is 256× larger, and nothing pins where the route/method/`401` decision sits relative to the body read (`http.rs` describes only "the request reader admits `Content-Length`-framed bodies within the budgets below"). Concrete failure: on the ADR's public-root posture (non-loopback bind, admin possibly disabled — the socket is still open), an anonymous caller sends 64 concurrent requests each claiming a 16,777,216-octet `Content-Length` body to any route, and a reader that runs before the router buffers and hands `serde_json` ~1 GiB in one std-only process. Deleting the per-record `source_keys` bound removes the old implicit key-count bound that the 64 KiB cap supplied.
findings.fix: One clause in `http.rs`/§Budgets: the router answers `404`/`405`/`401` from the header block alone, and a body claim on any route other than `POST /v1/admin/games` (whose legitimate bodies are always zero-length) is refused unread; state the worst-case inbound figure (`MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS` × body cap) beside the §Risks row it belongs to. Alternatively keep 65,536 as the non-admin body bound and bound `source_keys` per record, which retires the equality instead of widening it.

findings.location: §Test strategy #3 — "`025-B1`'s cap and §The serving face step 1's rule apply to **decoded** `slug` and decoded `DELETE` path segment"
findings.problem: The rewrite renamed the predicate but kept the wrong pair. A `026-C3` `game_id` is `is_slug_name(id) && len ≤ 128` (A4) and `is_slug_name` is `[a-z][a-z0-9-]*` with no `/` (crates/core/src/placement.rs:107), while `spells_lookup_key` requires a `/` (crates/discovery/src/game.rs:84, `split_once('/')`), so step 1's rule applied to a DELETE segment `404`s every valid `game_id`. Both authoritative texts, revised in this same diff, say otherwise: §The admin face pins "percent-decodes the path segment, validates the grammar (A4)", and step 1 now scopes its own rule to "candidate queries, admin upserts and cache loads alike" (DELETE absent). #3 therefore contradicts the two sections it exists to pin.
findings.fix: In #3 pin `slug` against `025-B1`'s cap plus §The serving face step 1's rule, and the `DELETE` path segment against the A4 grammar (`is_slug_name` + 128), keeping the separator/dot-dot/control-byte cases at the query seam.

findings.location: §Chosen design → `http.rs` — "a `Transfer-Encoding`, missing or non-decimal length, or an over-cap body is refused before any mutation" (and #11's "a `Transfer-Encoding`, `Content-Length`-less, or over-cap body is refused")
findings.problem:
This pass verified the contradicting fact into the register (A23: the shipped client sends one `GET` per connection carrying `Connection: close`), and the shipped request really is `GET …
Connection: close

` with no `Content-Length` (apps/discovery-cli/src/catalog.rs:438), yet the request-reader sentence still reads as refusing a missing length. Literally, the reader refuses every `GET /v1/candidates` — the primary route and the one `026-C1` requires to be byte-identical to what that client parses — so the framing rule keeps two readings at exactly the smuggling seam.
findings.fix: Name the zero-claim case so the refusal targets body claims only: `Transfer-Encoding` ⇒ refused; `Content-Length` present ⇒ read exactly that many octets within cap; absent ⇒ zero-length body.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets (request-budgets paragraph) — "`MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS` (= `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS`, so any record a loadable corpus could legally hold also fits an upsert and no per-record `source_keys` bound is needed)"
findings.problem: new/regression from this revision: the value reviewed in r1 was 65,536; the revision raises the admitted request body 256× to 16,777,216, and the paragraph's capacity accounting for MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS names only "≤64 live threads and ≤64 in-flight upstream hops", never admitted octets. The reader this design mirrors allocates the whole promised body once it clears the cap (apps/discovery-cli/src/catalog.rs:364 `vec![0u8; length]`), and the design never orders the admin auth check ahead of the body read ("an over-cap body is refused before any mutation" bounds mutation, not reading), so peak inbound reservation for the flagship 026-C5 routable root is 64 × 16 MiB ≈ 1 GiB plus the parsed value, for records that need kilobytes. The stated justification buys only the r1 round-trip consistency (a loaded record the admin face could never re-upsert); it does not price what it costs.
findings.fix: Either keep the equality and state what it implies — the admitted-octets bound 64 × `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS`, and that the auth check precedes the body read — or re-split the constants with a named per-record `source_keys` count cap chosen so one record fits a small `MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS` (65,536), refused by name in the `corpus.rs` refusal list and Test-strategy #1 (the alternative r1 offered).

findings.location: Chosen design → The admin face and auth, "Concurrency (open Q10)" — "a mutation serializes the new model, writes the fixed tmp name, renames it into place, and swaps the model in, **all under the one write lock** … A reader may wait on one local write, and that latency is accepted" — read against §Budgets "`MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` (16,777,216 — ≈120,000 records …)"
findings.problem: regression in scale: the r0 stall is now accepted rather than removed (the author's call, and the false "reads never wait on filesystem IO" claim is gone), but the same revision raised the document cap 16× from the 1 MiB this seat approved against, so "one local write" is now a whole-document serialize plus a write of up to 16 MiB held in the Corpus write lock, during which std::sync::RwLock admits no new shared reader — up to 63 of the 64 admitted connections queue behind one operator upsert on the root sized for ≈120,000 records. Neither §Concurrency nor the Risks low-and-slow row bounds the accepted wait, and #11's new "N concurrent upserts leave the persisted document equal to the model" pins ordering, not the reader's worst-case wait.
findings.fix: One clause naming the accepted wait as a number — "the write lock is held for one serialize plus one local write of at most `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS` octets; admin mutations are operator-rare on the root" — mirrored in the Risks row; or write the tmp outside the model write lock from the buffer prepared under it and take the lock only for the rename and model swap, keeping the ordering guarantee #11 tests.

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets (cache eviction paragraph) — "after a write the registry serializes the cache and re-serializes after each dropped entry — one extra pass per eviction at most — dropping the oldest-`fetched_at` entries … until the buffer is ≤ `026-B2` octets"
findings.problem: new in this revision: deleting the running totals moves the whole octet test onto the serialized buffer, and the parenthetical bounds passes-per-eviction but never bounds the number of evictions, which the loop condition leaves open. Reachable inside the design's own numbers: 026-B1's 5,000 entries at the paragraph's ~150–210-octet realistic size sit just under 1 MiB, so one saturated MAX_CANDIDATES answer (≈MAX_RESPONSE_OCTETS = 65,536, the figure this paragraph carried before the revision) forces dropping a few hundred thin entries, each drop triggering another full ~1 MiB re-serialization — O(evictions × document), hundreds of MiB serialized inside one cold-lookup request path. The text this diff replaces guaranteed the opposite ("O(1) plus evictions, never a whole-document re-serialization"), and #5 asserts only the end state, so nothing pins the cost.
findings.fix: Keep the exact-length test but stop re-serializing per drop: subtract each dropped entry's own serialized length (from the pass just taken) from a buffer total, drop until that total clears 026-B2, then serialize once and check the exact length, looping only if that check still fails; name the lock the write-through runs under in the same sentence.

findings.location: Caching mode → "Upstream reachability" — "probed **at most once per TTL**, fired lazily by the first *lookup* after expiry on that request's own thread"
findings.problem: re-raised, not a regression: dropping health reads as a driver narrows the window but leaves the hot case — concurrent cold lookups after expiry. The design still names no stamp or compare-and-set, so with one thread per admitted connection several of the 64 threads can pass the expiry test before a verdict stamp exists, making "at most once per TTL" intent rather than a property; each extra probe costs the mirrored 2 s connect / 5 s read on a serving thread, the very cost the Risks row "A cold caching registry's first scan is N serial upstream lookups" claims to mitigate. Compounded by `--refresh-interval <seconds>`, now specified as "a bare unsigned count of seconds" with no floor and pinned live at `1` by #6, far below those timeouts, degrading the bound toward a synchronous upstream probe per lookup.
findings.fix: One clause making the probe single-flight (the thread that compare-and-sets the `last_upstream_fetch` stamp is the only one that probes for that TTL; the rest serve the previous verdict) plus one clause stating the floor for `--refresh-interval` (at least the upstream read timeout).

findings.location: Chosen design → Budgets — "`fs::metadata`-gated before the read of the `--corpus` or local-entries file and refused by name (A22)"
findings.problem: re-raised: the third load path is still outside the gate — the cache's 026-B2 is only "re-checked at load", so as written an oversized `cache-v1.json` is read and parsed before refusal, while the ADR's 026-B2 says the cache file is "refused by name like the match store's", and both precedents the design invokes gate before allocating (matches.rs `load`/`STORE_READ_BUDGET_OCTETS`, A22; catalog.rs:353–364 checks the promise before `vec![0u8; length]`).

findings.location: apps/registry/src/serve.rs:206-215 with apps/registry/src/corpus.rs:218-231 (and apps/registry/src/constants.rs:15)
findings.problem: The serving face caps a candidate answer by count (MAX_CANDIDATES) but never by octets: constants.rs defines MAX_RESPONSE_OCTETS = 65_536 and its only uses are the inbound hop (upstream.rs:134/193), so write_response (http.rs:317-320) promises any body length. The format contract explicitly blesses records on every bound (schemas/catalog/v1/spec.md:78-80, fixtures/valid/on-every-length-bound.json), so 256 postings at game_id = 128 and name = 128 octets serialize to ≈71,900 octets, over 026-A1's body cap and over the shipped client's 5-digit Content-Length rule (apps/discovery-cli/src/catalog.rs:348): the shipped CLI then fails the scan with "the body promises N octets over the 65536-octet budget", and a caching registry turns the same legal root answer into stale/503 (upstream.rs:193-198). 026-C2 requires the answer to be within the budgets the shipped client pins (A1); the test that pins the count cap uses ~45-octet candidates (candidates_join.rs:135-178), so the gate never sees it.
findings.fix: Bound the answer by the same stable prefix: in candidates_answer (or Catalog::candidates) serialize and drop trailing postings while the body exceeds MAX_RESPONSE_OCTETS, keeping the first postings in game_id byte order so truncation stays stable, and pin it with a 256-record max-bound corpus; or record the acceptance in schemas/catalog/v1/spec.md and the run's risk record, since §Budgets reconciles 026-B1×026-B2 but never prices the response side.

findings.location: schemas/catalog/v1/spec.md:56-57 against apps/registry/src/corpus.rs:123-175 and :292-346
findings.problem: The shipped spec states "The entry set is closed: any other entry, a missing entry, or a wrong-typed entry is a named refusal", but the loader - the surface spec.md:10-15 names as this format's conformance surface - reads only the field names it wants and silently ignores extra entries at both document and record level (the admin upsert shares the same gate), so {"game_id":..,"name":..,"source_keys":[..],"gameId":"typo"} is accepted and stored. No fixtures/invalid/ case covers it (the 17 fixtures cover the other rows of the spec's refusal table), so nothing can catch the divergence.
findings.fix: Either reject unknown entries in from_document and record_from_value and ship the fixture the table row implies, or narrow the sentence to "a missing or wrong-typed entry is a named refusal; extra entries are ignored".

findings.location: apps/registry/src/corpus.rs:101-109 with apps/registry/src/main.rs:227-230
findings.problem: A root instance pointed at a nonexistent --corpus path starts and answers 200 [] for every slug. The "absent file is the empty document" rule is stated for the caching instance's local-entries document ("created empty if absent") and the cache (026-C7); extending it to --corpus turns an operator typo in a root's only content argument into a silently empty catalog instead of the named startup refusal every other corpus fault gets. No suite starts a root with a missing corpus.
findings.fix: Have State::root require the corpus file to exist (an explicit flag or a load parameter for absent-is-error), keeping absent-is-empty for the local-entries and cache documents, and pin it beside catalog_document.rs's other startup refusals.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/serve.rs:162-194
findings.problem: For a /v1/admin/** path, Dispatch::WrongMethod is answered (405 plus Allow) before enablement is consulted, so on a routable bind with no token - the state 026-C5 defines as admin disabled - PUT /v1/admin/stats and POST /v1/admin/games answer 405 with their method lists while every carried method answers 404. 026-C5 and §The admin face and auth say the disabled case is flatly 404 ("never a 401 oracle"); a 405+Allow is an existence oracle for a face the instance says it does not have. admin_auth.rs:14-16 shows the suite routed around this seam instead of covering it.
findings.fix: In admin_route, return the named 404 for every dispatch result when !admin.is_enabled(), keeping the 405/Allow behavior for an enabled face, and add one non-carried method to a_non_loopback_bind_without_a_token_disables_the_admin_face.

findings.location: apps/registry/** (new crate) and apps/discovery-cli/src/catalog.rs against 02-proposal.md:30-37 and docs/adrs/026-registry-service.md:245-248

findings.location: apps/registry/src/admin.rs:74-85
findings.problem: A parameterized path is treated as a route only for DELETE, so PUT/POST/GET /v1/admin/games/<valid-game-id> falls through Dispatch::NotARoute to a 404, while the collection path answers 405 with Allow: POST for a non-carried method. 026-C4's "A 405 names any method the route does not carry" reads onto the delete route too, so the two shapes are inconsistent.
findings.fix: Either answer 405 with Allow: DELETE once the segment is game_id-valid, or state the "parameterized paths are method-specific, everything else is 404" rule in spec.md/the route documentation so both shapes are deliberate.

findings.location: apps/registry/src (module list) and apps/registry/src/keys.rs:72-94
findings.problem: The crate adds four modules beyond the proposal's named nine-module file plan (keys.rs, persist.rs, state.rs, and a #[cfg(test)]-only wire.rs holding 599 lines of in-process wire suite in src/), and keys.rs re-expresses the lookup-key rule through Source::from_token rather than calling Source::spells_lookup_key, which §apps/registry names as the reused predicate. Both are behavior-equivalent.
findings.fix: Record the extra modules where the module list lives (or move wire.rs under tests/), and call spells_lookup_key directly so the closed-source-token reuse is one call rather than a reconstruction.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/main.rs:199-208
findings.problem: The missing-`<data>` startup refusal hard-codes "set `XDG_DATA_HOME` to an absolute path" even though the layout is resolved via `DataLayout::host()`; on the Windows branch (where `<data>` = absolute `%APPDATA%` per A6 and the matrix's Windows row) the message names a variable the platform rule never reads, and the unit test at main.rs:383-393 pins the Unix-only wording unconditionally.
findings.fix: Branch the refusal on the resolved layout: name `%APPDATA%` on the Windows branch (or name both spellings), and assert the wording that matches `DataLayout::host()` in the test.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/upstream.rs:72-73,102-105
findings.problem: `authority_of` (endpoint.rs:126) strips brackets from an IPv6 host and `fetch` rebuilds the authority as `format!("{host}:{port}")`, so an admitted bracketed IPv6 upstream (endpoint.rs:44-53, unit-pinned at endpoint.rs:146 for `http://[::1]:8080`) sends an unbracketed `Host: ::1:8080` — not the bracketed form RFC 9110 requires. It works only against this registry's own Host-blind reader; a standards-conforming front (proxy/vhost edge) can reject or misroute it.
findings.fix: Bracket the host when it contains ':' when building the Host header and authority string, e.g. `if host.contains(':') { format!("[{host}]:{port}") } else { format!("{host}:{port}") }`.

findings.location: apps/registry/tests/common/mod.rs:462-476
findings.problem: `Registry::caching` relocates the instance's documents via `XDG_DATA_HOME` alone while `Registry::start` scrubs `XDG_DATA_HOME`/`HOME`/`APPDATA` from every child (common/mod.rs:671-677). On a Windows host the child resolves `<data>` from the scrubbed `APPDATA`, finds none, and refuses to start — every caching-mode subprocess suite (cache_document, caching_policy, upstream_client, upstream_endpoint_gate, data_layout, cli_end_to_end caching legs) fails on the platform the Compatibility matrix marks supported. Test strategy #13 and the harness header (common/mod.rs:13-15) both name `APPDATA` as part of this same child-environment seam; Linux-only CI hides it.
findings.fix: In `Registry::caching`, set `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `HOME`, and `APPDATA` all to the sandbox directory (each layout ignores the other layouts' variables), making the helper portable and the #13 claim true for the whole suite.

findings.location: schemas/catalog/v1/fixtures/valid/ + apps/registry/tests/slug_decoding.rs:124-147
findings.problem: Every fixture and suite key/name is pure ASCII: the widened alphabet is pinned for dots, `%`, and spaces, but survival of a non-ASCII lookup key or display name (byte-wise percent-encode, octet-counted caps, UTF-8-validated decode) is only structurally true, never asserted.
findings.fix: Add one valid fixture with a non-ASCII external id (e.g. `local/Jörn`) plus a candidate-query row that round-trips it, and let the fixture-naming rule govern it.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/http.rs:310-329 (write_response); apps/registry/src/state.rs:253-279; apps/registry/src/cache.rs:136-171
findings.problem: No outbound response budget. constants.rs:31-33 says MAX_CANDIDATES is "the most candidates one answer may carry, in either direction", and the proposal's Goal (:21) plus §The serving face step 3 require the answer to stay inside A1's caps (body ≤ MAX_RESPONSE_OCTETS = 65_536, ≤ 256 candidates; 02-proposal.md:43,252; Test strategy #16's "caps"). Only Catalog::candidates truncates (corpus.rs:218-231); the cache-hit and stale paths return entry.candidates whole, Cache::load bounds no per-entry candidate list, and write_response measures nothing. A contract-valid corpus — 256 records riding the 128/128 bounds that fixtures/valid/on-every-length-bound.json declares loadable and sharing one source_key — answers 256×280+257 = 71,937 octets, which apps/discovery-cli's read_response refuses as over-budget (so the shipped CLI fails on a legal corpus, and a caching instance's own upstream reader turns a legal root answer into an upstream error and then a cold 503); separately, a cache document carrying thousands of candidates for one slug is served whole up to the 1 MiB 026-B2 size, per request. spec.md:101-103 waves at exactly this without closing the response seam, and no test pins it (response_shape.rs:236-239 uses a three-record corpus; candidates_join.rs:135-178 truncates short names only).
findings.fix: Cap the per-entry candidate list at the cache write seam (upstream.rs already refuses > MAX_CANDIDATES) and again at Cache::load as a named refusal, and measure the serialized candidate body against MAX_RESPONSE_OCTETS in candidates_answer/write_response, answering a named refusal (or narrowing the stable first-256 window) rather than emitting a body the pinned reader rejects. Add a wide corpus at the 128/128 bounds to tests/response_shape.rs and an over-cap cache entry to tests/cache_document.rs.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/main.rs:165-170 (flag arm at :154)
findings.problem: Only the space-separated spelling is parsed, so the common `--admin-token=S3CRET` form falls into the unknown-flag arm and prints "`--admin-token=S3CRET` is not a flag this registry has" to stderr (main.rs:65-68), writing the configured bearer token into terminal scrollback, journald or CI logs from one typo — checklist item 4's rule that no secret reaches a log line.
findings.fix: Split each argument on its first `=` and match the flag name (accepting or refusing `--admin-token=` by name), and echo only the flag name in the unknown-flag refusal, never the value; pin with a unit case asserting the refusal line omits the value.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/http.rs:234-260 (called at :161), with constants.rs:24-29 and :56
findings.problem: read_request reads the declared body before routing, and the enablement/admits checks happen only afterwards (serve.rs:162-191). An unauthenticated peer needs no valid token to make the server declare-and-buffer MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS = 16 MiB per connection — one per admitted slot, i.e. ~1 GiB of buffered body per burst of MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS = 64 sockets — before answering 401. The proposal sets the two budgets separately (§Budgets) and never takes their product as a pre-credential allowance.
findings.fix: Read the header block first and, for /v1/admin/**, decide is_enabled/admits from the already-complete headers and answer 401/404 before reading the declared body (close rather than drain); or give the admin upsert its own body cap well below the document cap and keep 16 MiB load-side only. Pin in tests/admin_auth.rs that an unauthenticated oversized POST is refused without consuming the body.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/admin.rs:111-118 and :210-222; apps/registry/src/serve.rs:162-194
findings.problem: With the defaults (--host 127.0.0.1, no token) the admin face is enabled and admits returns true for an uncredentialled request (admin.rs:134-136). POST /v1/admin/games parses its body as JSON whatever the Content-Type, and nothing checks Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site, so a simple cross-origin request — which needs no CORS preflight this server would answer — carries a full record. A page in a browser on the operator's own machine, DNS-rebound to 127.0.0.1, can blind-upsert into a caching instance's local-entries document, which by 026-L5 answers with zero upstream requests, is never merged and never expires: one write pins an attacker's game_id for a key the user's `discovery list` later trusts. Only the ephemeral default port and the unreadable response mitigate today.
findings.fix: Keep 026-C5's posture but close the browser path: require `Content-Type: application/json` on POST /v1/admin/games (a non-simple type, so a cross-origin caller must preflight and no OPTIONS route is answered), and refuse a carried admin request that carries an Origin header; pin both in tests/admin_auth.rs.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/http.rs:262-305 (find_header_end at :300-305)
findings.problem: read_header_block reads one octet at a time and calls find_header_end(&buffer) — bytes.windows(4).position(...) from offset 0 — after every octet. A maximal MAX_REQUEST_HEADER_OCTETS = 65,536 block costs ~2×10^9 4-byte comparisons (seconds of CPU) for 64 KiB of input, per connection, and the 60 s REQUEST_READ_TIMEOUT (constants.rs:67-71) lets the peer hold the admitted slot throughout. The design's own inbound budget thus becomes the cheapest network-to-CPU amplification available, against the low-and-slow exposure §Risks (02-proposal.md:456) claims those budgets bound; the crate's own upstream reader already does it linearly (upstream.rs:131 uses head.ends_with(b"\r\n\r\n")).
findings.fix: Test only the last four octets per iteration (buffer.ends_with(b"\r\n\r\n")) or resume the scan from buffer.len() - 4, keeping the cap check; add a bounded-time assertion to the request-budget case in tests/persist_and_concurrency.rs.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/persist.rs:194-218
findings.problem: save does write_all → flush → chmod → rename with no sync_all() on the tmp handle and no parent-directory sync. On a filesystem that does not order data before the rename's commit, a power loss can leave a zero-length or stale document for a mutation the admin face already answered 200 for, weakening §Concurrency's "a restart cannot lose an accepted mutation" (02-proposal.md:315-326) and checklist item 6's atomicity requirement. It mirrors the shipped matches.rs precedent, hence nit.
findings.fix: Call handle.sync_all() before dropping the handle (no-op branch on non-unix), optionally sync the parent after the rename, and pin the call in tests/persist_and_concurrency.rs; or state the durability limit in schemas/catalog/v1/spec.md's persistence paragraph.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/http.rs:262-305
findings.problem: read_header_block reads one byte per stream.read() syscall and, after every byte, rescans the entire accumulated buffer for \r\n\r\n via find_header_end (bytes.windows(4).position(...) from offset 0), making request-header parsing quadratic in a length the attacker chooses up to MAX_REQUEST_HEADER_OCTETS (65,536): a single preamble can cost ~5e8 window checks (~seconds of one core) plus 65,536 one-byte syscalls, and with MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS=64 a low-and-slow sender keeps up to 64 threads spinning quadratically. The duplicated-header check at http.rs:147-155 is O(h^2) over the same attacker-chosen block.
findings.fix: Make the terminator check incremental: after appending byte i, test only buffer[i-3..=i] (carry match state across appends) instead of rescanning from offset 0; read into a small chunked scratch buffer rather than one byte per syscall; check duplicates against a name set instead of scanning the header Vec.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/cache.rs:237-244
findings.problem: stage()'s octet-cap eviction loop runs a full O(n) min_by scan (cache.rs:284-296) plus a whole-document re-serialization per dropped entry, all while the cache write lock is held for stage->save->commit (state.rs:374-389). The proposal sanctions one extra pass per eviction, but a single staging can require hundreds of drops: with the document at the 1 MiB steady-state cap, one inserted entry at MAX_CANDIDATES (~23 KiB) can trigger ~150-300 full ~1 MiB serializations while every other lookup blocks on the cache read lock; tests/cache_document.rs:427 already exercises ~40 serializations in one call.
findings.fix: Measure per-entry serialized length once (or subtract incrementally), evict oldest until an estimate is under the cap with headroom, then serialize once and only re-loop if that single exact-buffer check still fails; replace the per-drop min_by scan with a running oldest-pointer.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/cache.rs:261-280
findings.problem: The cache document is serialized with to_string_pretty, inflating an ordinary one-candidate entry to ~250 octets against the proposal's ~150-octet budget arithmetic; ~4,000-4,500 ordinary entries already exceed MAX_CACHE_DOCUMENT_OCTETS (1,048,576), so 026-B2 evicts ordinary corpora before 026-B1's 5,000 cap — contradicting §Budgets' claim that '026-B1's 5,000 is the cap that binds ordinary answers' and cutting effective steady-state capacity by roughly a third, with each premature eviction also paying the eviction-loop cost.
findings.fix: Serialize the cache compactly (serde_json::to_vec), or, if legibility is intentional, record in schemas/catalog/v1/spec.md that 026-B2 (not 026-B1) binds ordinary corpora and restate the fit arithmetic.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/state.rs:253-278
findings.problem: On the caching fetch path, candidates() clones the same cache entry twice (cache.entry(slug).cloned() in step 2 for the fresh test and again in step 3 for the stale fallback), i.e. two full Vec<Candidate> clones (up to 256 Candidates) of the same entry per lookup, and maybe_probe (state.rs:331) takes the cache read lock a third time just for is_empty().
findings.fix: Take one read lock, do one slug lookup, test freshness from the single borrowed entry, and derive the probe-gating emptiness check from the same critical section.

findings.location: apps/registry/tests/response_shape.rs:236 (Test strategy #16 "caps" leg); apps/registry/src/corpus.rs:218; apps/registry/src/constants.rs:15
findings.problem: Nothing pins the answer against A1's MAX_RESPONSE_OCTETS = 65,536 cap, and the serving face never applies it: the outbound join is bounded only by MAX_CANDIDATES = 256 while game_id and name are each bounded at 128 octets (a bound the shipped valid fixture on-every-length-bound.json proves is inclusive), so a legal corpus whose key is claimed by ~250 max-bound records serializes to ~72,000 octets. The only octet assertion in the suite (response_shape.rs:236) runs against five tiny answers, and MAX_RESPONSE_OCTETS is documented as capping the header block and body yet is used solely by the inbound upstream client. Violates §The serving face ("wire traffic is per-slug candidate lists within 025 budgets") and Test strategy #16's shape clause; concrete failure: a root-mode answer of that size makes `discovery list --catalog-url` fail as `catalog unreachable` and makes a caching instance refuse its own upstream's legal answer (src/upstream.rs:193), so 026-C1's byte-identical face stops serving the client that pins it. Executed gate: `cargo test --workspace --locked` exit 0 (60 registry unit + 101 registry integration, all green), so no existing leg covers this.
findings.fix: Add a root-mode corpus of MAX_CANDIDATES records at the game_id/name bounds sharing one source key and assert the answer's framing satisfies the client (body <= MAX_RESPONSE_OCTETS); bound the outbound projection in octets (truncate the stable window further or answer a named refusal) so MAX_CANDIDATES truncation alone is not treated as sufficient, and state the arithmetic beside the cap in schemas/catalog/v1/spec.md.

findings.location: apps/registry/tests/caching_policy.rs:151-178 and apps/registry/tests/caching_policy.rs:326-364
findings.problem: Both fresh-cache legs seed fetched_at = now_unix() before the server subprocess is started, run with --refresh-interval 1, then assert the fresh behaviour (cache served, zero candidate requests to the fake). Their freshness budget is therefore 1 second of wall clock spanning spawn, the printed-port poll (tests/common/mod.rs:507) and the socket round trip; on a loaded runner the entry is legitimately stale by then, a refresh fires, the fake serves its [] default and the assertions fail for reasons unrelated to the code under test (checklist item 4: no wall-clock dependence).
findings.fix: Take the freshness stamp after the listener answers (seed the document before start, re-stamp once it is up) or run the fresh leg under the default 026-B3 TTL, reserving --refresh-interval 1 for the legs that must expire.

findings.location: apps/registry/tests/caching_policy.rs:326 (assertions at :358); apps/registry/tests/upstream_client.rs:343
findings.problem: The test is named for and documented as pinning #6's "re-times the once-per-TTL upstream probe", but it only counts GET /v1/candidates; the sole probe-count assertion in the suite (upstream_client.rs:343) measures a single default-TTL window and so proves only "at most one probe per TTL". An instance that caches the reachability verdict forever and never re-probes after expiry passes every current leg.
findings.fix: In the same test count upstream.lines_for("GET /v1/health") before the wait and after the second lookup and assert it grew by exactly one probe, keeping upstream_client.rs:314 for the "at most one" half.

findings.location: schemas/catalog/v1/fixtures/invalid/ (17 fixtures, none over-cap) vs Test strategy #1
findings.problem: #1 lists "document over MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS" among the conditions that "ships in fixtures/invalid/*.json as a named refusal", but no such fixture exists; the refusal is covered only by the loader suite (tests/catalog_document.rs:337), so an independent implementer running the golden fixtures never sees one of the two ends where §Budgets says the cap is enforced.
findings.fix: Reconcile the rosters in the contract: name MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS in schemas/catalog/v1/spec.md's refusal roster with a note that no fixture ships for the 16,777,216-octet cap and the refusal is pinned by apps/registry/tests/catalog_document.rs.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/constants.rs:71-75 (used at apps/registry/src/http.rs:386,392)
findings.problem: REQUEST_READ_TIMEOUT (60 s) and RESPONSE_WRITE_TIMEOUT (15 s) are wired and named in §Risks as the low-and-slow mitigation, but no leg observes them because their values make any test wait a minute — an untested knob (checklist item 7).
findings.fix: Expose the read timeout through a test seam (an undocumented --request-read-timeout <seconds>, or a constants override in serve.rs's unit tests) and add a leg asserting a connection that sends only a partial request is closed; otherwise record the knob as deliberately unlegged in 03-build-notes.md.

findings.location: apps/registry/src/serve.rs:124-131 (non-admin arm calls head.into_request before route), with apps/registry/src/http.rs:300-326 (read_body allocates vec![0u8; octets] for any method declaring a length) and apps/registry/src/constants.rs:29-32, 41-49
findings.problem:
Residual of my round-1 finding #3: the credential-before-body rule was applied to /v1/admin/** only. Any other path still has its declared body fully buffered before the route table is consulted, and no serving-face route ever reads a body (serve.rs:143-173 answers /v1/candidates and /v1/health from query_param and ignores request.body). An unauthenticated peer therefore still buys MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS = MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS = 16,777,216 octets of resident buffer per admitted connection: `GET /v1/health HTTP/1.1
Content-Length: 16777216

` across MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS = 64 slots is ~1.07 GiB of buffered data the server throws away — the same arithmetic as round 1, unchanged. The new constants.rs:41-49 comment states the general property that MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS "is never an unauthenticated peer's memory allowance", which the code holds only for the admin face; MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS is sized for the upsert's whole-document body, and the upsert is now the only route that parses a body at all. No green leg covers this: the new body-gate tests (tests/admin_auth.rs, src/wire.rs) exercise the admin path only.
findings.fix: Read a body only where a route parses one: move read_body behind the route table (pass a "this route parses a body" flag to into_request, or call it only from admin_connection's carried path), and for a route/method that parses none either refuse the Content-Length or discard it via drain_unread_body. findings.location: apps/registry/src/constants.rs:51-53 and apps/registry/src/http.rs:386-399 (drain_unread_body)
findings.problem: The new comment states "A peer that stops sending a body it declared holds the admitted slot for this long and no longer" (2 s), but UNREAD_BODY_DRAIN_TIMEOUT is a socket read timeout, so it expires only on a gap between octets: a peer that declared Content-Length: 65536 and dribbles one octet every ~1.99 s keeps the drain loop alive for ~65,536 iterations (tens of hours), holding one of the 64 slots. Pre-existing and larger on the body-read path (read_body's read_exact at http.rs:321-324 with REQUEST_READ_TIMEOUT = 60 s against a 16 MiB declaration), and the change strictly reduces the refused-request ceiling from 16 MiB to 64 KiB, so this is only a budget comment promising a bound the mechanism does not provide.
findings.fix: Either give a drained (or body-read) connection an absolute deadline — track an Instant and stop after a stated total, e.g. UNREAD_BODY_DRAIN_TIMEOUT x 8 — or reword the comment to what the code does (a gap of that long ends the discard), matching REQUEST_READ_TIMEOUT's honest "does not police idle peers" wording.

findings.location: apps/registry/tests/cli_end_to_end.rs:512-556 (helper at apps/registry/tests/common/mod.rs:1048-1054)
findings.problem: New in this increment: the explicit-`--port` leg takes the port it binds from `closed_loopback_port()`, a helper whose stated contract is "the 'no reachable upstream' of `026-L4`" — it binds a loopback listener, reads the assigned port, and drops it. Used as a port to re-bind in a child, the value is free only until something else takes it: with the test binary's parallel threads, a concurrent `FakeUpstream`/`SteamRoot` `bind("127.0.0.1:0")` can be handed the just-learned port before the child binds it, and the leg then dies at startup (common/mod.rs:512-517 panics on the child exiting before printing a port). Linux's rotating ephemeral allocator makes the coincidence rare — hence nit, and the gate is green — but reuse of a recently closed port is the documented behavior on the matrix's Windows row, where this leg is claimed supported and never run.
findings.fix: Stop borrowing the unreachable-upstream helper for a bind: hold the probe listener until just before `Registry::start` and retry the child start once with a freshly learned port if the bind is taken, or drive the leg from a per-test port in a range no `bind(:0)` in this binary can be handed.

findings.location: §The serving face step 1 — "Percent-decode `slug` **first**, then apply `025-B1`'s 128-octet cap and `spells_lookup_key` to the *decoded* bytes", read with the r3 space admission ("no control byte or invalid-UTF-8 sequence")
findings.problem: The widened alphabet makes an unspecified part of the decode seam load-bearing. The copied `percent_encode` (A19, verified at apps/discovery-cli/src/catalog.rs:174-185) never emits a bare `+` and escapes `+` as `%2B`, so a percent-decode that also folds `+` to a space (the form-urlencoding habit) turns a shipped-legitimate `local/foo+bar` into `local/foo bar`. Before the space ban was deleted that mistranslation died loudly at the seam; now it yields a legal key, which caching mode then forwards `%20`-encoded (step 4) and caches under, answering a different question than it was asked. The design never authorizes `+`-folding, so this is underspecification introduced by the closure of my own finding, not a contradiction.
findings.fix: In step 1, pin the decode to percent-escapes only: "percent-decode (a literal `+` stays `+`; the only space spelling is `%20`, as the copied `percent_encode` emits)". One parenthetical; #3's `404` list and the outbound hop are unchanged by it.

findings.location: §Budgets → request budgets — "`MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS` (= `MAX_CATALOG_DOCUMENT_OCTETS`, so any record a loadable corpus could legally hold also fits an upsert and no per-record `source_keys` bound is needed)"
findings.problem: The revision moved the inbound request-body bound from the r1 value this seat approved (65,536, "mirroring the client's own header cap") to 16,777,216 for every route, because the constant was re-purposed as the document cap; the §Risks row still cites it as the inbound mitigation ("Low-and-slow / one-inbound-per-outbound exposure on a routable bind … `MAX_REQUEST_HEADER_OCTETS`/`MAX_REQUEST_BODY_OCTETS`") while the bound it names is 256× larger, and nothing pins where the route/method/`401` decision sits relative to the body read (`http.rs` describes only "the request reader admits `Content-Length`-framed bodies within the budgets below"). Concrete failure: on the ADR's public-root posture (non-loopback bind, admin possibly disabled — the socket is still open), an anonymous caller sends 64 concurrent requests each claiming a 16,777,216-octet `Content-Length` body to any route, and a reader that runs before the router buffers and hands `serde_json` ~1 GiB in one std-only process. Delet… [elided by the checkpoint cap]
findings.fix: One clause in `http.rs`/§Budgets: the router answers `404`/`405`/`401` from the header block alone, and a body claim on any route other than `POST /v1/admin/games` (whose legitimate bodies are always zero-length) is refused unread; state the worst-case inbound figure (`MAX_CONCURRENT_CONNECTIONS` × body cap) beside the §Risks row it belongs to. Alternatively keep 65,536 as the non-admin body bound and bound `source_keys` per record, which retires the equality instead of widening it.

findings.problem: The rewrite renamed the predicate but kept the wrong pair. A `026-C3` `game_id` is `is_slug_name(id) && len ≤ 128` (A4) and `is_slug_name` is `[a-z][a-z0-9-]*` with no `/` (crates/core/src/placement.rs:107), while `spells_lookup_key` requires a `/` (crates/discovery/src/game.rs:84, `split_once('/')`), so step 1's rule applied to a DELETE segment `404`s every valid `game_id`. Both authoritative texts, revised in this same diff, say otherwise: §The admin face pins "percent-decodes the path segment, validates the grammar (A4)", and step 1 now scopes its own rule to "candidate queries, admin upserts and cache loads alike" (DELETE absent). #3 therefore contradicts the two sections it exists to pin.
findings.fix: In #3 pin `slug` against `025-B1`'s cap plus §The serving face step 1's rule, and the `DELETE` path segment against the A4 grammar (`is_slug_name` + 128), keeping the separator/dot-dot/control-byte cases at the query seam.

findings.location: §Chosen design → `http.rs` — "a `Transfer-Encoding`, missing or non-decimal length, or an over-cap body is refused before any mutation" (and #11's "a `Transfer-Encoding`, `Content-Length`-less, or over-cap body is refused")
findings.problem:
This pass verified the contradicting fact into the register (A23: the shipped client sends one `GET` per connection carrying `Connection: close`), and the shipped request really is `GET …
Connection: close

` with no `Content-Length` (apps/discovery-cli/src/catalog.rs:438), yet the request-reader sentence still reads as refusing a missing length.
